text: When evaluating an author's merit and determining their place among our most revered figures, we are entitled to assess them from our own perspective and measure them against our own standards. However, in evaluating the power displayed in their works, we must consider their own intentions and compare their creations to their ideal, noting what is lacking. We differ from Mr. Poe in our views on the objectives of art, as he believes the primary goal is to create Beauty, although our disagreement may stem from differing definitions of this term. Nonetheless, in our discussion of his writings, we will adhere to his own standards. The realm of the god of song is accessible from all sides, and there is ample space for all who bring offerings or seek guidance. In his stories, Mr. Poe has chosen to demonstrate his skill primarily in the realm that lies between the boundaries of probability and the realm of superstition and unreality. He possesses a rare combination of faculties, blending the ability to influence the reader's mind with the subtle suggestions of mystery and a meticulous attention to detail that overlooks nothing. Both of these qualities are, in fact, natural consequences of the dominant characteristic of his mind, which is analysis. This analytical mind enables the artist to focus on the intended effect, making all elements subordinate to the central goal. Even his mysterious elements are subject to mathematical precision in his own mind, where the unknown quantity is always known. When he creates a picture, he is aware of the chemical properties of all the colors he uses, and although some of his figures may seem vague or formless, their outlines are as clear to him as a geometric diagram. This is why Mr. Poe has no affinity for Mysticism, which immerses itself in mystery and allows it to permeate all thoughts. In contrast, Mr. Poe approaches his subject from the outside, analyzing, dissecting, and observing with a serene eye the intricate mechanisms at work. This analytical tendency balances his poetic inclinations, granting him the patience to be meticulous and infuse his most fanciful creations with a sense of reality. He is particularly skilled at portraying monomania, dissecting the subtle roots of these mental afflictions with great power. He also excels at evoking images of horror, often conveying a sense of terrible doubt through subtle hints, leaving the imagination to complete the picture, a task for which it is uniquely suited. As it is said, 'much imaginary work was there; Conceit deceitful, so compact, so kind, That for Achilles' image stood his spear Grasped in an armed hand; himself behind Was left unseen, save to the eye of mind.'

text: My primary objective is to establish a magazine, to be titled 'The Stylus,' but it would be of little value to me if it were not entirely under my control, free from the influence of a publisher. To achieve this, I intend to create a journal that is truly my own in every aspect. With this goal in mind, I must secure a list of at least five hundred subscribers before launching the magazine; I have already gathered nearly two hundred. I plan to travel to the South and West to meet with my personal and literary acquaintances, including old college and West Point friends, to see what support I can garner. To raise the necessary funds for the initial step, I propose to deliver a lecture at the Society Library on Thursday, February 3rd, and to avoid any potential controversy, my topic will not be literary in nature. I have chosen a broad and universal subject: 'The Universe.' Having presented you with the facts of the matter, I leave the rest to your discretion and generosity. I am deeply grateful. Your friend always, EDGAR A. POE. Although these letters are brief and hastily written, they demonstrate the presence of qualities often denied to Mr. Poe, such as humility, perseverance, and a capacity for genuine and grateful friendship. These traits were undoubtedly characteristic of him when he was sane, and they have consistently been our experience of him throughout our five- or six-year friendship. It is easier to believe what we have personally witnessed than what we have only heard, and so we remember him with admiration and respect; the descriptions of him during periods of moral insanity seem to us like portraits of a man we have only known in health, painted during times of sickness. However, there is another, more poignant and compelling evidence of the goodness in Edgar A. Poe. To reveal this, we must delicately lift the veil that shields the grief and refinement of those living in poverty, but we believe it is justified if it can help to illuminate the poet's memory, and it may also serve a more immediate and necessary purpose in the aftermath of his death. Our first knowledge of Mr. Poe's move to this city came when a lady introduced herself as the mother of his wife and visited us, seeking employment for him. She explained that he was ill, her daughter was a confirmed invalid, and their circumstances were such that she felt compelled to take action. The lady's countenance, radiant with a selfless devotion to a life of hardship and sorrowful tenderness, her gentle and mournful voice, her refined yet understated manners, and her appreciative mention of her son's abilities, all revealed a truly angelic presence, one of those extraordinary women who rise above adversity. It was a difficult fate that she was struggling to overcome, as Mr. Poe's writing, though meticulous and refined, was not well-suited to the popular taste and therefore not well-rewarded.

I also placed a pair of pigeons and a cat in the car. As daybreak was approaching, I deemed it time to depart. While pretending to pick up a lit cigar I had dropped, I discreetly ignited the slow match that protruded slightly from one of the smaller casks. This action went unnoticed by the three men nearby, and I quickly jumped into the car, cut the cord that tied me to the ground, and was pleased to find that I ascended effortlessly, carrying 175 pounds of leaden ballast with ease and capable of carrying just as much more. One night, or rather early in the morning of the murder, he returned home from a night out with other sailors and found the orangutan in his bedroom, where it had broken in from a closet where it was supposed to be securely locked. The animal was sitting in front of a mirror, trying to shave itself with a razor, having apparently watched its owner do so through the keyhole. Terrified by the sight of such a dangerous weapon in the hands of a ferocious animal, the man was at a loss for what to do. However, he had experience calming the creature down with a whip, so he used that. As soon as the orangutan saw the whip, it jumped out of the room, down the stairs, and out a window that was unfortunately open, into the street.

The Frenchman followed in desperation; the orangutan, still holding the razor, would occasionally stop and look back at its pursuer, gesturing at him, until the Frenchman was about to catch up.

St. Eustache, Marie's lover and intended husband, who lived with her mother, claimed he was unaware of the discovery of his intended's body until the following morning. It was then that M. Beauvais entered his room and informed him of the news. The reception of this news seemed surprisingly subdued, given its significance. The journal attempted to convey the impression that Marie's relatives were apathetic about her disappearance, which would be inconsistent with the idea that they believed the recovered body to be hers. The journal's insinuations suggested that Marie had left the city with the knowledge of her friends, due to a scandal involving her reputation, and that upon finding a similar-looking corpse, her friends took the opportunity to deceive the public into believing she was dead. However, L'Etoile was too hasty in its accusations. It was proven that the supposed apathy did not exist; the elderly lady was extremely frail and agitated, unable to attend to her duties. St. Eustache, far from being calm, was overcome with grief and behaved frantically, prompting M. Beauvais to ask a friend to take charge of him and prevent him from attending the disinterment examination. Furthermore, despite L'Etoile's claims that the corpse was reburied at public expense, that the family declined a private burial offer, and that no family member attended the ceremony, all these assertions were disproven. In a later issue, the paper attempted to cast suspicion on Beauvais himself. The editor stated that on one occasion, while Madame B—— was visiting Madame Rogêt, M. Beauvais, upon leaving, instructed her not to speak to the expected gendarme until he returned. It seemed that M. Beauvais had taken control of the entire matter, and for some reason, he was determined to be the only one involved in the proceedings, even going so far as to push the male relatives aside in a peculiar manner. He appeared to be strongly opposed to allowing the relatives to see the body. A circumstance that lent some credibility to the suspicion against Beauvais was the discovery, by a visitor to his office a few days before Marie's disappearance, of a rose in the keyhole and the name 'Marie' written on a nearby slate, while Beauvais was absent.

text: To me, this article seems to reveal more about the enthusiasm of its writer than anything else. We must remember that newspapers often prioritize creating a stir and making a point over pursuing the truth. The truth is only sought when it aligns with the goal of creating a sensation. An article that simply echoes common opinion, no matter how well-founded, does not impress the masses. The general public tends to regard as insightful only those who propose provocative contradictions to the prevailing idea. In reasoning, just as in literature, it is the clever phrase that is most immediately and widely appreciated, even if it is of relatively low merit. What I am saying is that it is the combination of clever phrasing and dramatic flair in the idea that Marie Rogêt is still alive, rather than any genuine plausibility, that has led L'Etoile to propose it and made it appealing to the public. Let us examine the key points of this journal's argument, trying to clarify the incoherent way it was originally presented. The writer's primary goal is to demonstrate that, given the short time between Marie's disappearance and the discovery of the floating corpse, the corpse cannot be Marie's. The writer's eagerness to minimize this time interval leads to hasty assumptions from the start. The writer claims, 'It is foolish to suppose that the murder, if it occurred, could have been committed quickly enough for the murderers to throw the body into the river before midnight.' We naturally ask, why is this assumption foolish? Why is it unreasonable to think that the murder could have taken place within five minutes of the girl leaving her mother's house, or at any other time of day? There have been murders at all hours. Even if the murder had occurred at any moment between 9 am on Sunday and a quarter before midnight, there would still have been enough time to throw the body into the river before midnight. This assumption essentially means that the murder did not occur on Sunday at all. If we allow L'Etoile to make this assumption, we might as well permit any other liberties. The paragraph that begins 'It is foolish to suppose that the murder...' can be imagined to have originally been thought by its writer as 'It is foolish to suppose that the murder could have been committed soon enough to enable the murderers to throw the body into the river before midnight; it is foolish, we say, to suppose all this and at the same time suppose that the body was not thrown in until after midnight,' a sentence that is inconsequential in itself but not as absurd as the printed version. Were my intention simply to critique this part of L'Etoile's argument, I could safely leave it as it is.

With the profound awareness of their responsibility towards the being they had brought into the world, combined with their innate kindness, it can be inferred that during my early years, I was constantly taught valuable lessons in patience, charity, and self-control. As a result, my life seemed like a continuous stream of joy, guided by a gentle and unobtrusive influence. For a considerable period, I was the sole focus of their attention. My mother had always desired a daughter, but I remained their only child. When I was around five years old, my parents took a trip beyond the Italian borders and spent a week by the shores of Lake Como. Their compassionate nature often led them to visit the humble homes of the poor, which, for my mother, was not just a duty, but an essential part of her being, driven by the memories of her own struggles and the relief she had received. On one of their walks, they came across a small, impoverished cottage in a valley, which caught their attention due to its extreme poverty and the large number of half-clothed children surrounding it. One day, while my father was away in Milan, my mother and I visited this cottage. Inside, she found a hardworking peasant and his wife, struggling to provide for their five children. Among them was a child who stood out from the rest, with a distinctly different appearance. The other four children had dark eyes and appeared robust, while this child was slender and remarkably fair, with hair that shone like gold and a face that seemed to radiate an otherworldly beauty. Her features were so expressive of kindness and sensitivity that it was impossible not to regard her as a unique and special being. The peasant woman, noticing my mother's fascination with the child, eagerly shared her story. The girl was not her own, but the daughter of a nobleman from Milan, whose mother had been a German and had died in childbirth. The child had been placed in the care of this family, who had been better off at the time and had only recently had their own child. The girl's father had been a passionate advocate for Italian liberty, but his efforts had ultimately led to his downfall, and his fate remained unknown. His property had been seized, leaving his child an orphan and a beggar. Despite the humble surroundings, the child had thrived with her foster family, blossoming like a rose among thorns. When my father returned from Milan, he found a beautiful child playing with me in the hall of our villa, a creature who seemed to emanate light and joy, with a form and movements as gentle as a mountain goat.

With this deep awareness of what they owed to the being they had brought into the world, combined with the active spirit of tenderness that drove both of them, it's easy to imagine that during every hour of my early life, I received lessons in patience, charity, and self-control. She remembered what she had gone through and how she had been helped, and she felt compelled to pay it forward by being a guardian angel to those in need. On one of their walks, they noticed a small, rundown cottage in a valley that seemed particularly desperate, with a large number of poorly dressed children gathered around it, clearly struggling with poverty. One day, when my father had gone to Milan on his own, my mother and I visited this home. She found a hardworking peasant and his wife, worn down by their struggles, trying to feed their five hungry children. Among them was one child who caught my mother's attention more than any of the others. This child seemed to be from a different background altogether. The other four children had dark eyes and were robust, but this child was thin and very fair-skinned. Her hair was a vibrant, golden blonde, and despite her tattered clothing, it seemed to give her an air of distinction. Her forehead was clear and broad, her blue eyes were bright and clear, and her lips and facial features expressed a deep sensitivity and sweetness that made it impossible for anyone to look at her without seeing her as someone special, a being with a heavenly quality to her. The peasant woman noticed that my mother was staring at this beautiful girl in wonder and admiration, and she eagerly shared the child's story. The girl was not her own child, but the daughter of a nobleman from Milan. Her mother, a German woman, had died in childbirth, and the baby had been placed with this family to be cared for. At the time, they were better off, having only recently married and having just had their first child. The girl's father was one of those Italians who had been inspired by the country's past glory and had fought for its freedom. He had become a victim of the country's weaknesses and was either dead or still imprisoned in an Austrian dungeon. His property had been seized, and his child had been left an orphan and a beggar. Despite this, she had thrived with her foster family, blossoming in their simple home like a rose among dark-leaved thorns. When my father returned from Milan, he found a child playing with me in the hall of our villa - a child who was even more beautiful than the cherubs depicted in art, radiating joy and lightness, with a form and movements as agile as a mountain goat.

My parents were very aware of their responsibility to me, and they both had a strong sense of kindness and compassion. As a result, I learned important lessons about patience, charity, and self-control from a very young age. My parents guided me gently, and everything seemed enjoyable to me. We found a poor family with many children, and one of the children stood out to my mother. This child was different from the others, with fair hair and blue eyes. Despite being poorly dressed, she seemed special. My mother was very taken with this child and wanted to know more about her. The woman of the house told us that the child was not hers, but the daughter of a nobleman from Milan. Her mother had been German and had died in childbirth. The child had been left with this family to care for, but now they were struggling to make ends meet. The child's father had been involved in the fight for Italian freedom and had lost everything. When my father returned from Milan, he found me playing with this child in our villa. She was even more beautiful than I had described, and her presence seemed to light up the room.

A sense of calm and joy filled my soul as I abandoned my long-standing and recently troubling studies. This marked the beginning of my association of evil with pursuing such studies and happiness with abandoning them. However, this attempt to break free from my destiny was unsuccessful, as the unyielding laws of fate had already decreed my downfall. When I turned seventeen, my parents decided it was time for me to attend the University of Ingolstadt. Before I could leave, disaster struck - Elizabeth contracted scarlet fever, and her condition was critical. Many people tried to persuade my mother not to care for her, but when she heard Elizabeth's life was in danger, she couldn't resist her anxiety. My mother's devoted care ultimately saved Elizabeth, but at a terrible cost: she fell ill herself. On her deathbed, my mother showed remarkable strength and kindness. Elizabeth, you must take my place and care for your younger siblings.' She accepted her fate and died peacefully, her face still filled with love. The pain of losing a loved one is indescribable - the void it leaves, the despair it brings, and the struggle to accept that they are truly gone. It takes time for the reality of the loss to sink in, and the true bitterness of grief to set in. But who hasn't experienced such a loss, and why should I describe a sorrow that everyone must endure?

The spirit of Frankenstein exclaimed, I have accomplished so much, but I will achieve far more, blazing a new trail and uncovering the secrets of creation by building upon the discoveries already made. I will explore uncharted powers and reveal to the world the deepest mysteries of existence. That night, I could not sleep, my mind was in a state of turmoil, and I felt that a new order would emerge from the chaos, but I was powerless to bring it about. As the morning dawned, sleep finally came, and when I awoke, my thoughts from the previous night seemed like a dream. All that remained was a firm resolve to return to my old studies and devote myself to a field in which I believed I had a natural aptitude. On the same day, I visited M. Waldman, and I found his private demeanor to be even more gentle and charming than his public persona, as the dignity he displayed during his lectures gave way to kindness and affability in his own home. I gave him a similar account of my previous pursuits as I had given to his colleague, and he listened attentively to my brief narrative about my studies, smiling at the mention of Cornelius Agrippa and Paracelsus, but without the disdain that M. Krempe had shown. He remarked that these men, although their zeal was sometimes misdirected, had laid the foundations for modern philosophers, and that their discoveries, although not always properly understood, had ultimately benefited humanity. He said that they had left behind a legacy of knowledge, which we could build upon, giving new names to their discoveries and organizing them into a coherent system. I listened to his words, which were spoken without pretension or affectation, and then expressed my gratitude for his lecture, which had dispelled my prejudices against modern chemists. I spoke with restraint, showing the modesty and respect due to a youth towards his instructor, and I asked for his advice on the books I should acquire. M. Waldman replied, I am delighted to have gained a student, and if your dedication matches your ability, I have no doubt you will succeed. Chemistry, he said, is the branch of natural philosophy where the greatest advances have been made, and it is the field I have chosen to specialize in, but I have not neglected other areas of science. A person who focuses solely on chemistry would make a poor chemist, for to be a true man of science, one must be well-versed in all branches of natural philosophy, including mathematics. He then took me to his laboratory, where he explained the purpose of his various instruments, instructing me on what I should acquire and offering me the use of his own equipment when I had progressed far enough in my studies. He also provided me with the list of books I had requested, and I took my leave.

So much has been accomplished, exclaimed the soul of Frankenstein - more, far more, will I achieve; building on the foundation already laid, I will blaze a new trail, explore uncharted powers, and reveal to the world the deepest secrets of creation.

My father's letters contained no criticism, only a more detailed inquiry into my activities, which he had not done before. As the seasons passed - winter, spring, and summer - I was completely absorbed in my work, oblivious to the blossoming flowers and expanding leaves that had once brought me such joy. By the time the leaves withered, my project was nearing completion, and each day revealed the success of my endeavours. However, my excitement was tempered by anxiety, making me seem more like a slave toiling in a mine than an artist passionate about his craft. Every night, I suffered from a lingering fever, and my nerves were on edge to the point of pain; even the sound of a falling leaf startled me, and I avoided human contact as if I were guilty of some transgression. Occasionally, I was alarmed by the state I had become, but the drive to complete my work sustained me, and I convinced myself that once it was finished, I could regain my health through exercise and leisure. My creation would soon be complete, and I looked forward to a time when I could indulge in both. It was a dismal November night when I finally saw the culmination of my efforts. With an anxiety that bordered on anguish, I gathered the tools necessary to imbue life into the inanimate being at my feet. It was already past one in the morning, the rain drummed against the windows, and my candle was almost spent when, by the faint light, I saw the creature's dull yellow eye open; it breathed laboriously, and its limbs convulsed. I am at a loss to describe my emotions at this moment or to portray the being I had painstakingly created. Its limbs were proportionate, and I had chosen its features for their beauty. But, oh God, its yellow skin barely concealed the underlying muscles and arteries, its hair was a lustrous black, and its teeth were a pearly white; however, these features only served to accentuate the horror of its watery eyes, which seemed to match the colour of the dull-white sockets that held them, its shrivelled skin, and straight black lips. The unpredictability of life's events is nothing compared to the volatility of human emotions. I had toiled for nearly two years, driven by an all-consuming passion to animate an inanimate body, sacrificing rest and health in the process. But now that my goal was achieved, the allure of my dream dissipated, replaced by an overwhelming sense of horror and disgust. Unable to bear the sight of the being I had created, I fled the room and paced back and forth in my bedchamber for a long time, trying to calm my mind and find sleep. Eventually, exhaustion took over, and I collapsed onto my bed, still dressed, seeking a brief respite from my turmoil.

My father didn't criticize me in his letters, but he did notice my silence by asking more specific questions about what I was doing. However, my excitement was tempered by my anxiety, and I felt more like someone forced into hard labor than an artist doing what they loved. Every night, I felt overwhelmed by a low-grade fever, and I became extremely nervous; even the sound of a leaf falling would startle me, and I avoided being around other people as if I had done something wrong. Sometimes I was alarmed by the state I had gotten myself into, but the only thing that kept me going was my determination to finish. I thought that once my work was done, I could relax and have some fun, and that would help me recover from the stress I was under. I promised myself that I would take a break and enjoy myself once my creation was complete. It was a gloomy November night when I finally saw the result of my hard work. I was extremely anxious, almost to the point of agony, as I gathered the equipment I needed to bring my creation to life. It was already 1 am, the rain was coming down against the windows, and my candle was almost out. Just as the light was fading, I saw the creature's dull yellow eye open; it was breathing heavily, and its limbs were convulsing. I'm not sure how to describe my feelings at that moment, or how to portray the being I had worked so hard to create. Its limbs were proportional, and I had chosen its features carefully, trying to make them beautiful. But its yellowish skin was almost transparent, showing the muscles and blood vessels underneath; its hair was black and shiny, but its eyes were a watery color that seemed to match the pale sockets they were set in. The creature's complexion was dry and wrinkled, and its lips were thin and black. Life is unpredictable, but human emotions can change even more quickly. I had spent nearly two years working tirelessly to bring a lifeless body to life. I had given up rest and health for this goal, and I had wanted it so badly that it had become an obsession. But now that it was finished, the dream had lost its appeal, and I was filled with horror and disgust. I couldn't bear to look at the being I had created, so I ran out of the room and paced back and forth in my bedroom for a long time, unable to calm down. Eventually, I became exhausted and lay down on the bed in my clothes, trying to forget what I had just experienced.

Before, these things would have brought me great joy, but now I was too caught up in what I was doing. By the time my project was almost finished, the leaves had already started to wither and fall. Every day, I could see that I was getting close to succeeding, but my excitement was mixed with worry. I felt like I was trapped in a never-ending job, like working in a mine, rather than doing something I loved. Sometimes, I realized how much my health had suffered, but I kept going because I knew my work would be done soon. I told myself that once it was finished, I could rest and have some fun, and that would make me feel better.

My minor pursuits keep me occupied and entertained, and I am rewarded for my efforts by seeing only happy and kind faces around me. One change has occurred in our household since your departure. Madame Moritz, Justine's mother, was a widow with four children, and Justine was the third. Although Justine was her father's favorite, her mother, for some inexplicable reason, could not stand her and treated her poorly after her father's death. My aunt noticed this and, when Justine was twelve, persuaded her mother to let her live with us. The democratic institutions of our country have fostered simpler and more pleasant manners than those found in the surrounding monarchies. As a result, there is less distinction between social classes, and the lower classes are neither as impoverished nor as despised, leading to more refined and moral behavior. In Geneva, being a servant does not carry the same connotations as it does in France and England. My homeland, my cherished land, how delightful it was to once again behold your rivers, mountains, and most of all, your enchanting lake. As I approached my home, however, sorrow and fear overcame me, and the night's darkness deepened my despair. The scene before me seemed a vast, ominous landscape, and I foresaw a bleak future, destined to become the most miserable of humans. Alas, my prophecy proved true, but I had not imagined even a fraction of the anguish that awaited me. Upon arriving in the vicinity of Geneva, I found the town gates closed, and I was forced to spend the night in the village of Secheron, half a league from the city. The sky was clear, but I couldn't rest, so I decided to visit the spot where my poor brother William had been murdered. To get there, I had to cross the lake by boat to reach Plainpalais. During this brief journey, I saw lightning dancing on the summit of Mont Blanc in breathtaking patterns. The storm was approaching rapidly, and after landing, I climbed a small hill to observe its progress. The heavens grew cloudy, and the rain began to fall in large drops, quickly intensifying. I left my perch and walked on, despite the increasing darkness and storm, as the thunder boomed above me. The sound was echoed by the surrounding mountains, and flashes of lightning illuminated the lake, making it seem like a vast expanse of fire, only to plunge everything into darkness again. The storm, typical of those in Switzerland, seemed to rage in multiple parts of the sky at once. The most violent tempest hung over the lake, between the promontory of Belrive and the village of Copêt, while another storm faintly illuminated the Jura, and yet another shrouded the Môle, a peaked mountain to the east. As I watched the tempest, both beautiful and terrifying, I wandered on with hasty steps. The turmoil in the sky lifted my spirits, and I exclaimed aloud, 'William, dear angel, this is your funeral, your dirge!' As I spoke, I noticed a figure emerging from behind a cluster of trees near me. I stood frozen, gazing intently, and a flash of lightning revealed the object's shape, its gigantic stature and hideous deformity, unmistakably the creature I had brought to life. What was it doing there? Could it be, I shuddered at the thought, the murderer of my brother?

Everyone was talking about the murder, but the captain interrupted and said, 'Be careful, the current is strong here, and the body might have washed up and gotten stuck in the bushes by the water's edge. I hope that's what happened.'

I didn't want that to happen. Everyone on the boat leaned over the side, looking really closely, but they couldn't see me. Then the captain shouted, 'Stand back!' and the cannon fired right in front of me, making me temporarily deaf and blind from the smoke. I thought I was in trouble, but luckily I wasn't hurt. The boat floated away and disappeared around the island. I could hear the cannon firing every now and then, but it got fainter and eventually stopped. The island is three miles long, and I thought they had reached the end and given up. But they didn't. They turned around and started going up the channel on the other side of the island, firing the cannon occasionally.

When they got to the top of the island, they stopped firing and went to the other shore, heading back to town. I knew I was safe now. No one else would be looking for me. I took my things out of the canoe and set up a camp in the woods. I made a tent out of my blankets to keep my things dry, and I caught a catfish and cooked it for supper. As the sun began to set, I started a fire and ate my meal.

I thought I could land almost anywhere, but it wasn't that easy - the bank was too steep. I was nearly at the foot of the island before I found a suitable spot. I decided to head into the woods, figuring it was pointless to mess with rafts as long as they were moving the lantern around. I had my pipe, some dog-leg tobacco, and matches in my cap, which weren't wet, so I was all set.

Every night, around ten o'clock, I'd sneak ashore in some small village and buy a little food, like meal or bacon, for ten or fifteen cents; sometimes I'd even snatch a chicken that wasn't roosting too comfortably and take it with me. Pap always said that if you get the chance to take a chicken, you should, because even if you don't want it yourself, you can always find someone who does, and a good deed is never forgotten. Although I never saw Pap turn down a chicken himself, that's what he always said, anyway.

In the mornings, before daylight, I'd slip into cornfields and take a watermelon, or a mushmelon, or a pumpkin, or some fresh corn. Pap claimed it wasn't wrong to borrow things as long as you planned to pay them back someday, but the widow said that was just a nice way of saying stealing, and no respectable person would do it. Jim thought the widow was partly right and Pap was partly right, so he suggested we pick a few things from the list and decide not to borrow them anymore, and that way it wouldn't be wrong to borrow the rest. We spent one whole night discussing it, drifting down the river, trying to decide whether to give up watermelons, cantaloupes, or mushmelons. By dawn, we'd made up our minds and decided to stop taking crabapples and persimmons. We felt better after that, and I was glad we'd made that decision, since crabapples are never any good, and persimmons wouldn't be ripe for a couple of months yet.

Now and then, we'd shoot a bird that got up too early or stayed up too late. All in all, we were living pretty well.

On the fifth night after passing St. Louis, a big storm rolled in after midnight, with a lot of thunder and lightning, and the rain came down in sheets. We huddled in the wigwam and let the raft take care of itself. When the lightning flashed, we could see a long, straight stretch of river ahead, with high, rocky bluffs on both sides. After a while, I said, 'Hey, Jim, look over there!' It was a steamboat that had run aground on a rock. We were drifting straight for it. The lightning showed it to us in perfect detail. The boat was tilted to one side, with part of its upper deck above water, and we could see every little chimney and a chair by the big bell, with an old slouch hat hanging on the back of it, whenever the lightning flashed.

Well, it being the middle of the night, and stormy, and all so mysterious, I felt just like any other boy would when I saw that wreck lying there, so sad and lonely in the middle of the river. I wanted to sneak aboard and snoop around a bit, to see what was there. So I said, 'Let's land on her, Jim.'

But Jim was against it at first. He said, 'I don't want to go fooling around any wreck.'

I asked Jim, “Am I, or am I not? You tell me this: Didn’t you take out the line in the canoe to tie up to the tow-head?” Jim replied, “No, I didn’t. What tow-head are you talking about? I haven’t seen any tow-head.” I pressed him, “You haven’t seen any tow-head? Look, didn’t the line come loose and the raft drift down the river, leaving you and the canoe behind in the fog?” Jim seemed puzzled, “What fog are you talking about?” I clarified, “The fog that’s been around all night. Didn’t we shout, and didn’t you shout, until we got mixed up in the islands and one of us got lost, and the other was just as good as lost because he didn’t know where he was? And didn’t I crash into a lot of those islands and have a terrible time, almost getting drowned? Isn’t that what happened, Jim? Tell me.” Jim responded, “This is all too much for me, Huck. I haven’t seen any fog, or islands, or troubles. I’ve been sitting here talking with you all night until you fell asleep about ten minutes ago, and I think I did the same. You couldn’t have gotten drunk in that time, so you must have been dreaming.” Jim was skeptical, “How could I have dreamed all that in just ten minutes?” I insisted, “You must have dreamed it, because none of it actually happened.” Jim thought for a moment, “But, Huck, it all seems so clear to me...” I interrupted, “It doesn’t matter how clear it seems; it’s just not true. I know, because I’ve been here the whole time.” Jim was quiet for about five minutes, thinking it over. Then he said, “Well, I reckon I did dream it, Huck; but I swear, it’s the most powerful dream I’ve ever had. And I’ve never had a dream before that’s left me feeling so tired.” I reassured him, “Well, that’s okay, because sometimes a dream can exhaust you just like anything else. But this one was a really vivid dream; tell me all about it, Jim.” So Jim started telling me the whole story, just as it had happened in his dream, although he embellished it quite a bit. After that, he wanted to interpret the dream, because he believed it was a warning. He said the first tow-head represented a man who would try to help us, but the current symbolized another man who would try to take us away from him. The shouts we heard were warnings that would come to us from time to time, and if we didn’t try to understand them, they would lead us into bad luck instead of keeping us out of it. The many tow-heads signified the troubles we would face with quarrelsome and mean people, but if we kept to ourselves and didn’t provoke them, we would get through the difficulties and out of the fog, into the clear river, which represented the free states, where we would no longer have any trouble. The sky had darkened a bit after I got on the raft, but it was starting to clear up again. I asked Jim, “That’s a good interpretation, Jim, but what do these other things mean?”

We set off on the raft after dark. Anyone who still doesn't believe that handling a snake-skin is foolish after all it's done for us will likely change their mind after reading on and seeing what else it did for us. The best place to find canoes is near rafts tied up at the shore, but we didn't see any, so we continued on for over three hours. As the night wore on, it grew gray and somewhat thick, similar to fog, making it difficult to see the river's shape or any distance. It became very late and still, and then a steamboat came upstream. We lit the lantern, thinking they would see it. Boats traveling upstream usually kept their distance from us, following the bars and searching for calm water under the reefs, but on nights like this, they would push right up the channel. We could hear the boat approaching, but didn't see it clearly until it was close. It seemed to be heading straight for us. Often, boats would try to see how close they could get without touching, and sometimes the wheel would bite off a sweep, prompting the pilot to laugh and think himself clever. This boat, however, didn't appear to be veering off. It was large and moving quickly, resembling a black cloud with rows of glow-worms, but then it loomed big and intimidating, with a long row of open furnace doors shining like red-hot teeth, and its massive bows and guards hanging over us. There was a yell, a jingling of bells to stop the engines, a flurry of curses, and a whistle of steam, and as Jim jumped into the water on one side and I on the other, the boat smashed through the raft. I dove, aiming to reach the bottom, as a thirty-foot wheel needed to pass over me, and I wanted to give it plenty of room. I could usually hold my breath for a minute, but this time I stayed under for about a minute and a half. Then I quickly swam to the surface, as I was about to burst. I emerged up to my armpits, blew water out of my nose, and puffed a bit. The current was strong, and the boat started its engines again just ten seconds after stopping, as they didn't care much for raftsmen. Now the boat was churning along up the river, out of sight in the thick weather, although I could still hear it. I called out for Jim about a dozen times, but got no response, so I grabbed a plank that floated by and struck out for the shore, pushing it ahead of me. However, I realized the current was drifting towards the left-hand shore, which meant I was in a crossing, so I changed direction and headed that way.

There was a picture of a young woman standing at a window, gazing up at the moon with tears streaming down her face. She was holding an open letter with a black seal and clutching a locket to her mouth. The picture was captioned 'And Art Thou Gone Yes Thou Art Gone Alas.' I thought these pictures were nice, but they always gave me the shivers when I was feeling down. Everyone was sad that the artist had passed away, as she had planned to create many more works like these. You could see from what she had already done what a great loss it was. I figured that, given her temperament, she was probably happier in the graveyard. She was working on what was supposed to be her masterpiece when she fell ill, and she prayed every day and night to be allowed to live long enough to finish it. The picture showed a young woman in a long white dress, standing on the edge of a bridge, ready to jump, with her hair flowing down her back and tears running down her face. She had multiple arms folded across her chest, stretched out in front of her, and reaching up towards the moon - the idea was to decide which set of arms looked best and then erase the rest. However, she died before making up her mind, and now the picture hung over her bed, adorned with flowers on her birthday and hidden behind a curtain at other times. The woman in the picture had a sweet face, but all those arms made her look a bit too strange to me. This young artist used to keep a scrapbook, where she would paste obituaries, accidents, and stories of suffering from the Presbyterian Observer, and then write her own poetry about them. Her poetry was really good. For example, she wrote a poem about a boy named Stephen Dowling Bots who fell down a well and drowned. The poem went like this: ODE TO STEPHEN DOWLING BOTS, DEC’D. It asked if young Stephen had fallen ill and died, and if the people around him were sad and crying. But that wasn't what happened to Stephen Dowling Bots. He didn't die from whooping cough or measles, and he wasn't struck down by unrequited love or stomach troubles. No, his fate was different. He fell down a well, and by the time they pulled him out, it was too late. His spirit had already left this world and gone to a better place.

The following Sunday, we all attended church, which was about three miles away, with everyone riding horseback. The men brought their guns along, just like Buck did, and kept them between their knees or leaned them against the wall. The Shepherdsons did the same thing. The sermon was quite unpleasant, focusing on brotherly love and similar topics that seemed tedious, but everyone praised it as a good sermon. On the way home, they all discussed it, talking about faith, good deeds, and predestination, among other things, which made it seem like one of the most unpleasant Sundays I had experienced.

About an hour after dinner, everyone was dozing off, either in their chairs or in their rooms, and the atmosphere became quite dull. Buck and a dog were lying on the grass in the sun, fast asleep. I went up to my room, thinking I would take a nap as well. As I passed by, I saw Miss Sophia standing in her doorway, which was next to ours. She invited me into her room, closed the door softly, and asked if I liked her. I replied that I did, and then she asked if I would do something for her without telling anyone. I agreed, and she told me she had left her Testament at church, between two other books, and asked if I could sneak out and retrieve it for her without saying anything to anyone. I agreed to do so.

I slipped out and made my way to the church, where I found no one except maybe a few hogs, as there was no lock on the door and hogs like to stay on the puncheon floor during summer because it's cool. It's interesting to note that most people only attend church when they have to, but hogs are different. As I thought to myself, something seemed unusual; it wasn't normal for a girl to be so worried about a Testament. So, I shook it, and a small piece of paper fell out with '_Half-past two_' written on it in pencil. I searched the Testament but couldn't find anything else. The paper didn't make sense to me, so I put it back in the book and headed home.

When I got upstairs, Miss Sophia was waiting for me in her doorway. She pulled me into her room, closed the door, and then looked in the Testament until she found the paper. As soon as she read it, she looked happy, and before I could react, she grabbed me and gave me a squeeze, saying I was the best boy in the world and telling me not to tell anyone. Her face turned red, and her eyes sparkled, making her look very pretty. I was quite surprised, but once I caught my breath, I asked her what the paper meant. She asked if I had read it, and I said no. Then she asked if I could read writing, and I told her I could only read coarse handwriting. She said the paper was just a bookmark to keep her place, and I could go play now.

She asked if I had read it, and I said no. Then she asked if I could read writing, and I said only basic handwriting. She told me the paper was just a bookmark to keep her place, and I could go play now.

Jim claimed it was spirits, but I disagreed, saying spirits wouldn't use phrases like 'Dern the dern fog.' As soon as night fell, we set off, and when we reached the middle of the river, we let the current take us wherever it wanted. We'd light our pipes, dangle our legs in the water, and talk about various things. We usually went naked, both day and night, as long as the mosquitoes allowed it. The new clothes Buck's family made for me were too nice to be comfortable, and besides, I wasn't too fond of clothes anyway. Sometimes we'd have the entire river to ourselves for a long time. Over yonder, we'd see the banks and islands, and maybe a spark of light from a candle in a cabin window. On the water, we might see a spark or two from a raft or scow, and occasionally we'd hear the sound of a fiddle or a song coming from one of those crafts. Living on a raft was lovely. We'd gaze up at the starry sky and discuss whether the stars were created or just happened to be there. Jim thought they were made, but I believed they just happened. I figured it would take too long to create so many stars. Jim suggested that the moon could have laid them, which seemed somewhat reasonable, so I didn't argue against it. After all, I'd seen a frog lay almost as many eggs, so it was possible. We'd also watch the shooting stars and see them streak across the sky. Jim thought they'd been thrown out of the nest because they'd gone bad. On certain nights, we'd see a steamboat gliding through the darkness, and occasionally it would spew out a cloud of sparks from its chimneys, which would rain down into the river and look beautiful. Then it would turn a corner, its lights would disappear, and the noise would stop, leaving the river quiet once again. Later, its waves would reach us, rocking the raft gently, and after that, we wouldn't hear anything for a long time, except maybe the sound of frogs. After midnight, the people on shore would go to bed, and for a few hours, the shores would be dark, with no more sparks in the cabin windows. Those sparks served as our clock - the first one to reappear would signal that morning was approaching, so we'd quickly find a place to hide and tie up. One morning, just before daybreak, I found a canoe and crossed over a chute to the main shore, which was only about two hundred yards away. I paddled about a mile up a creek surrounded by cypress woods, looking for some berries. As I was passing a spot where a kind of cowpath crossed the creek, I saw two men running up the path as fast as they could. I thought I was in trouble, figuring that whenever someone was chasing someone, it was probably me - or maybe Jim.

Jim thought it was ghosts, but I said, 'No way, ghosts wouldn't say, "Dern the dern fog."' As soon as it got dark, we pushed off and let the current take us wherever it wanted. We'd just float, smoke our pipes, and hang our legs over the side of the raft, talking about all sorts of things. We were always naked, day and night, as long as the mosquitoes didn't bother us too much. The new clothes Buck's family had made for me were too nice to be comfortable, and to be honest, I wasn't really into clothes anyway. Sometimes we'd have the whole river to ourselves for hours. You could see the banks and islands across the water, and occasionally a light from a cabin window or a raft. You might even hear someone playing a fiddle or singing. It was amazing to live on a raft. We'd lie on our backs and stare up at the stars, debating whether they were created or just happened to be there. Jim thought they were made, but I thought they just happened. I figured it would have taken too long to make that many. Jim said the moon could have laid them, which seemed kind of reasonable, so I didn't argue. I mean, I've seen a frog lay a lot of eggs, so it's possible. We'd also watch the shooting stars and see them streak across the sky. Jim thought they were stars that had gone bad and got thrown out of the sky. A few times a night, we'd see a steamboat gliding through the darkness, and sometimes it would shoot out a bunch of sparks from its chimneys. The sparks would rain down into the river and look really cool. Then the boat would turn a corner, its lights would disappear, and everything would be quiet again. After a while, the waves from the boat would reach us and rock the raft a bit. For a long time after that, all you'd hear would be frogs or something. After midnight, the people on shore would go to bed, and the shores would be dark for a few hours. We used the lights from the cabin windows as a kind of clock - when we saw the first light of the morning, we'd find a place to hide the raft right away. As I was passing a spot where a path crossed the creek, I saw two men running down the path as fast as they could. I thought I was in trouble, figuring they must be after me or Jim.

As I was passing a place where a path crossed the stream, I saw two men running down the path as fast as they could. I thought I was in trouble, thinking that they might be after me or Jim.

It nearly killed Jim with laughter. He was always the easiest person to make laugh. I took the watch, and Jim lay down and started snoring; eventually, the storm subsided completely, and when the first cabin light appeared, I woke him up, and we hid the raft for the day. After breakfast, the king pulled out an old, worn-out deck of cards, and he and the duke played a game of seven-up for a while, betting five cents per game. When they got tired of it, they decided to come up with a new plan. The duke rummaged through his carpet-bag and pulled out a bunch of small, printed bills, which he read aloud. One of the bills announced that the 'celebrated Dr. Armand de Montalban, of Paris' would be giving a lecture on phrenology at a certain location, with admission costing ten cents, and character charts available for twenty-five cents each. The duke claimed to be this person. Another bill introduced him as the 'world-renowned Shakespearian tragedian, Garrick the Younger, of Drury Lane, London.' Other bills listed various names and accomplishments, including finding water and gold with a divining rod and breaking witch spells. The duke then said, 'But the theater is my true passion. Have you ever acted on stage, Your Majesty?' The king replied that he hadn't. The duke told him, 'You will, then, before you're three days older. The first decent town we come across, we'll rent a hall and perform the sword fight from Richard III and the balcony scene from Romeo and Juliet. What do you think?' The king agreed, saying he was willing to do anything that would pay, but he didn't know much about acting and hadn't seen many plays. The duke assured him it would be easy to learn. The king was eager to start, so the duke began explaining the story of Romeo and Juliet, saying he would play Romeo and the king could play Juliet. The king expressed concern that his appearance might not be suitable for the role, given his age and balding head. The duke dismissed his worries, saying that the audience wouldn't notice, and that costumes would make all the difference. He produced a few old curtain-calico suits, which he claimed were medieval armor, and a long white cotton nightshirt and ruffled nightcap for the king to wear as Juliet. The king was satisfied, so the duke read the parts aloud in a dramatic fashion, acting out the scenes to demonstrate how it should be done. Then, he handed the book to the king and told him to memorize his lines. There was a small town about three miles down the river, and after dinner, the duke said he had figured out a way to travel during the day without putting Jim in danger. He decided to go into town to make the necessary arrangements.

So the duke told him all about who Romeo was and who Juliet was, and said he was used to playing Romeo, so the king could be Juliet. 'But if Juliet's such a young girl, duke, my bald head and my white whiskers are going to look pretty odd on her, maybe.' 'Don't worry; these country people won't think twice about that. The people had abandoned their homes. The riverbank had given way under some of the houses, leaving one corner of them hanging precariously. Although people still lived in them, it was a perilous existence, as large chunks of land could collapse into the river at any moment. In fact, it was not uncommon for a stretch of land as wide as a house to cave in all at once. Sometimes, a long strip of land would start to collapse and continue to do so until the entire section had fallen into the river by the end of the summer. As a result, the town was constantly being forced to move backward, away from the river's relentless erosion. The river was always eating away at the town, which meant that the town had to keep moving back, and back, and back. As the day wore on, the streets became increasingly crowded with wagons and horses, and more were arriving all the time. Families had brought their lunches with them from the country and were eating in their wagons. There was a significant amount of whiskey being consumed, and I witnessed three fights. Suddenly, someone shouted, 'Here comes old Boggs, in from the country for his monthly binge! Here he comes, boys!' The idlers all seemed pleased, and I assumed they were accustomed to having a good time at Boggs' expense. One of them remarked, 'I wonder who he'll be picking a fight with this time. If he had actually fought all the men he's threatened to over the past twenty years, he'd have quite a reputation by now.' Another one said, 'I wish old Boggs would threaten me, because then I'd know I wasn't going to die for a thousand years.' Boggs came riding into town on his horse, whooping and yelling like a wild man, and shouting, 'Clear the track, I'm on the warpath, and the price of coffins is going to rise!' He was drunk and swaying in his saddle, a man over fifty with a very red face. Everyone jeered at him and laughed at him, and he retorted, saying he'd get to them eventually and take care of them one by one, but for now, he had to attend to Colonel Sherburn, whom he had come to town to kill. His motto, he claimed, was 'Meat first, and then dessert.' When he spotted me, he rode over and asked, 'Where are you from, boy? Are you ready to die?' Then he rode on. I was frightened, but a man reassured me, 'Don't worry, he doesn't mean anything. He's always carrying on like that when he's drunk. He's the kindest old fool in Arkansas, and he's never hurt anyone, whether he's sober or drunk.' Boggs reined in his horse in front of the largest store in town, leaned down to look under the awning, and yelled, 'Come out here, Sherburn! Come out and face the man you've cheated! You're the one I'm after, and I'm going to get you too!' He continued to rant and rave, calling Sherburn every name in the book, while the crowd packed the street, listening and laughing. Eventually, a dignified-looking man of about fifty-five, who was also the best-dressed man in town, emerged from the store. The crowd parted to let him through, and he said to Boggs in a calm, slow voice, 'I'm tired of this, but I'll put up with it until one o'clock.'

The people had moved out of the houses. The bank had collapsed under one corner of some of the others, and that corner was now hanging over the edge. People still lived in them, but it was hazardous because sometimes a large section of land would suddenly give way. Sometimes a huge chunk of land, a quarter of a mile deep, would start to collapse and keep going until it all fell into the river in just one summer. A town like that has to constantly move back because the river is always eroding it. The crowd started to jeer at the man and make fun of him, which made him angry, and he began to struggle and cause a commotion. This stirred up the crowd, and many men started to get down from the benches and rush towards the ring, shouting, 'Knock him down! Throw him out!' A few women also started to scream. The ring-master then gave a short speech, saying he hoped there wouldn't be any trouble, and if the man promised to behave, he would let him ride the horse if he thought he could stay on. Everyone laughed and agreed, and the man got on the horse. As soon as he was on, the horse started to buck and jump around, with two circus men holding onto its bridle, trying to control it, while the drunk man held onto the horse's neck, his heels flying in the air with each jump. The entire crowd was on its feet, shouting and laughing until tears streamed down their faces. Eventually, the horse broke free, and it galloped around the ring with the drunk man lying on its back, holding onto its neck, and the crowd went wild. I wasn't amused, though - I was worried sick about the man's safety. However, soon he managed to pull himself up and grab the bridle, swaying from side to side, and the next moment, he jumped up, dropped the bridle, and stood up on the horse's back, which was still galloping wildly. He stood up there, moving effortlessly, as if he were sober, and then he started to take off his clothes and throw them away. He shed so many clothes that they filled the air, and in total, he removed seventeen suits. Finally, he was left standing there, looking slim and handsome, dressed in the most colorful and attractive outfit, and he started to whip the horse, making it run even faster. He eventually jumped off, bowed, and danced off to the dressing room, and the crowd was ecstatic. The ring-master realized he had been fooled, and he was the most upset ring-master I had ever seen. It turned out that the drunk man was one of his own performers, and he had planned the whole thing without telling anyone. I felt foolish for being deceived, but I wouldn't have wanted to be in the ring-master's place for anything. I don't know if there are better circuses out there, but this one was good enough for me, and I would always go back to it if I had the chance. That night, we had our own show, but there were only about twelve people in the audience, just enough to cover our expenses. They laughed throughout the performance, which made the duke angry, and everyone left before the show was over, except for one boy who was asleep.

We were headed for a big city like Louis or Cincinnati, and the king told me to grab a steamboat, saying we'd meet up in the village later. I didn't need to be told twice to take a steamboat ride. I made my way to the shore about half a mile above the village and then followed the bluff bank in the calm water. Before long, we came across a young man sitting on a log, wiping the sweat from his face. It was extremely hot, and he had a couple of large carpet-bags beside him. The king instructed me to steer the boat towards the shore, which I did. 'Where are you headed, young man?' the king asked. 'I'm going to catch the steamboat to Orleans,' the young man replied. 'Get on board,' the king said. 'Wait a minute, my servant will help you with those bags.' The king meant me, and I got out to assist the young man. We all three continued on our way then. The young fellow was very grateful, saying it was a struggle to carry his luggage in such heat. He asked the king where he was going, and the king explained that he had come down the river and landed at the other village that morning. Now, he was going to visit an old friend at a farm a few miles up the river. The young man said, 'When I first saw you, I thought to myself, 'That's Mr. Wilks, and he's just made it in time.' But then I thought, 'No, it can't be him, or he wouldn't be paddling up the river.'' The king replied, 'No, my name is Blodgett - Reverend Elexander Blodgett, to be precise, since I'm one of the Lord's servants. Still, I'm just as able to feel sorry for Mr. Wilks for not arriving on time, if he's missed anything.' Joe whispered to me, “I’d give a shilling if they had cut and run,
Pip.”

We were joined by no stragglers from the village, for the weather was
cold and threatening, the way dreary, the footing bad, darkness coming
on, and the people had good fires in-doors and were keeping the day. A
few faces hurried to glowing windows and looked after us, but none came
out. We passed the finger-post, and held straight on to the churchyard.
There we were stopped a few minutes by a signal from the sergeant’s
hand, while two or three of his men dispersed themselves among the
graves, and also examined the porch.

I leaned over Joe, and, with the aid of my forefinger read him the
whole letter.

“Astonishing!” said Joe, when I had finished. “You ARE a scholar.”

“How do you spell Gargery, Joe?” I asked him, with a modest patronage.

“I don’t spell it at all,” said Joe.

“But supposing you did?”

“It _can’t_ be supposed,” said Joe. “Tho’ I’m uncommon fond of reading,
too.”

“Are you, Joe?”

“On-common. Give me,” said Joe, “a good book, or a good newspaper, and
sit me down afore a good fire, and I ask no better. Lord!” he
continued, after rubbing his knees a little, “when you _do_ come to a J
and a O, and says you, ‘Here, at last, is a J-O, Joe,’ how interesting
reading is!”

I derived from this, that Joe’s education, like Steam, was yet in its
infancy. Pursuing the subject, I inquired,—

“Didn’t you ever go to school, Joe, when you were as little as me?”

“No, Pip.”

“Why didn’t you ever go to school, Joe, when you were as little as me?”

“Well, Pip,” said Joe, taking up the poker, and settling himself to his
usual occupation when he was thoughtful, of slowly raking the fire
between the lower bars; “I’ll tell you. My father, Pip, he were given
to drink, and when he were overtook with drink, he hammered away at my
mother, most onmerciful. It were a’most the only hammering he did,
indeed, ’xcepting at myself. And he hammered at me with a wigor only to
be equalled by the wigor with which he didn’t hammer at his
anwil.—You’re a listening and understanding, Pip?”

“Yes, Joe.”

“Consequence, my mother and me we ran away from my father several
times; and then my mother she’d go out to work, and she’d say, “Joe,”
she’d say, “now, please God, you shall have some schooling, child,” and
she’d put me to school. But my father were that good in his hart that
he couldn’t abear to be without us. So, he’d come with a most
tremenjous crowd and make such a row at the doors of the houses where
we was, that they used to be obligated to have no more to do with us
and to give us up to him. And then he took us home and hammered us.
Which, you see, Pip,” said Joe, pausing in his meditative raking of the
fire, and looking at me, “were a drawback on my learning.”

“Certainly, poor Joe!”

“Though mind you, Pip,” said Joe, with a judicial touch or two of the
poker on the top bar, “rendering unto all their doo, and maintaining
equal justice betwixt man and man, my father were that good in his
hart, don’t you see?”

I didn’t see; but I didn’t say so.

“Well!” Joe pursued, “somebody must keep the pot a-biling, Pip, or the
pot won’t bile, don’t you know?”

I saw that, and said so.

“Consequence, my father didn’t make objections to my going to work; so
I went to work at my present calling, which were his too, if he would
have followed it, and I worked tolerable hard, I assure _you_, Pip. In
time I were able to keep him, and I kep him till he went off in a
purple leptic fit. And it were my intentions to have had put upon his
tombstone that, Whatsume’er the failings on his part, Remember reader
he were that good in his heart.”

“You say nothing of her,” remarked Miss Havisham to me, as she looked
on. “She says many hard things of you, but you say nothing of her. What
do you think of her?”

“I don’t like to say,” I stammered.

“Tell me in my ear,” said Miss Havisham, bending down.

“I think she is very proud,” I replied, in a whisper.

“Anything else?”

“I think she is very pretty.”

“Anything else?”

“I think she is very insulting.” (She was looking at me then with a
look of supreme aversion.)

“Anything else?”

“I think I should like to go home.”

“And never see her again, though she is so pretty?”

“I am not sure that I shouldn’t like to see her again, but I should
like to go home now.”

“You shall go soon,” said Miss Havisham, aloud. “Play the game out.”

Saving for the one weird smile at first, I should have felt almost sure
that Miss Havisham’s face could not smile. It had dropped into a
watchful and brooding expression,—most likely when all the things about
her had become transfixed,—and it looked as if nothing could ever lift
it up again. Her chest had dropped, so that she stooped; and her voice
had dropped, so that she spoke low, and with a dead lull upon her;
altogether, she had the appearance of having dropped body and soul,
within and without, under the weight of a crushing blow.

I played the game to an end with Estella, and she beggared me. She
threw the cards down on the table when she had won them all, as if she
despised them for having been won of me.

“When shall I have you here again?” said Miss Havisham. “Let me think.”

I was beginning to remind her that to-day was Wednesday, when she
checked me with her former impatient movement of the fingers of her
right hand.

“There, there! I know nothing of days of the week; I know nothing of
weeks of the year. Come again after six days. You hear?”

“Yes, ma’am.”

“Estella, take him down. Let him have something to eat, and let him
roam and look about him while he eats. Go, Pip.”

I followed the candle down, as I had followed the candle up, and she
stood it in the place where we had found it. Until she opened the side
entrance, I had fancied, without thinking about it, that it must
necessarily be night-time. The rush of the daylight quite confounded
me, and made me feel as if I had been in the candlelight of the strange
room many hours.

“You are to wait here, you boy,” said Estella; and disappeared and
closed the door.

I took the opportunity of being alone in the courtyard to look at my
coarse hands and my common boots. My opinion of those accessories was
not favourable. They had never troubled me before, but they troubled me
now, as vulgar appendages. I determined to ask Joe why he had ever
taught me to call those picture-cards Jacks, which ought to be called
knaves. I wished Joe had been rather more genteelly brought up, and
then I should have been so too.

She came back, with some bread and meat and a little mug of beer. She
put the mug down on the stones of the yard, and gave me the bread and
meat without looking at me, as insolently as if I were a dog in
disgrace.

“Well, miss?” I answered, almost falling over her and checking myself.

She stood looking at me, and, of course, I stood looking at her.

“Am I pretty?”

“Yes; I think you are very pretty.”

“Am I insulting?”

“Not so much so as you were last time,” said I.

“Not so much so?”

“No.”

She fired when she asked the last question, and she slapped my face
with such force as she had, when I answered it.

“Now?” said she. “You little coarse monster, what do you think of me
now?”

“I shall not tell you.”

“Because you are going to tell upstairs. Is that it?”

“No,” said I, “that’s not it.”

“Why don’t you cry again, you little wretch?”

“Because I’ll never cry for you again,” said I. Which was, I suppose,
as false a declaration as ever was made; for I was inwardly crying for
her then, and I know what I know of the pain she cost me afterwards.

We went on our way upstairs after this episode; and, as we were going
up, we met a gentleman groping his way down.

“Whom have we here?” asked the gentleman, stopping and looking at me.

“A boy,” said Estella.

He was a burly man of an exceedingly dark complexion, with an
exceedingly large head, and a corresponding large hand. He took my chin
in his large hand and turned up my face to have a look at me by the
light of the candle. He was prematurely bald on the top of his head,
and had bushy black eyebrows that wouldn’t lie down but stood up
bristling. His eyes were set very deep in his head, and were
disagreeably sharp and suspicious. He had a large watch-chain, and
strong black dots where his beard and whiskers would have been if he
had let them. He was nothing to me, and I could have had no foresight
then, that he ever would be anything to me, but it happened that I had
this opportunity of observing him well.

“Boy of the neighbourhood? Hey?” said he.

“Yes, sir,” said I.

“How do _you_ come here?”

“Miss Havisham sent for me, sir,” I explained.

“Well! Behave yourself. I have a pretty large experience of boys, and
you’re a bad set of fellows. Now mind!” said he, biting the side of his
great forefinger as he frowned at me, “you behave yourself!”

With those words, he released me—which I was glad of, for his hand
smelt of scented soap—and went his way downstairs. I wondered whether
he could be a doctor; but no, I thought; he couldn’t be a doctor, or he
would have a quieter and more persuasive manner. There was not much
time to consider the subject, for we were soon in Miss Havisham’s room,
where she and everything else were just as I had left them. Estella
left me standing near the door, and I stood there until Miss Havisham
cast her eyes upon me from the dressing-table.

“So!” she said, without being startled or surprised: “the days have
worn away, have they?”

“Yes, ma’am. To-day is—”

“There, there, there!” with the impatient movement of her fingers. “I
don’t want to know. Are you ready to play?”

I was obliged to answer in some confusion, “I don’t think I am, ma’am.”

Then, he and my sister would pair off in such nonsensical speculations
about Miss Havisham, and about what she would do with me and for me,
that I used to want—quite painfully—to burst into spiteful tears, fly
at Pumblechook, and pummel him all over. In these dialogues, my sister
spoke to me as if she were morally wrenching one of my teeth out at
every reference; while Pumblechook himself, self-constituted my patron,
would sit supervising me with a depreciatory eye, like the architect of
my fortunes who thought himself engaged on a very unremunerative job.

In these discussions, Joe bore no part. But he was often talked at,
while they were in progress, by reason of Mrs. Joe’s perceiving that he
was not favourable to my being taken from the forge. I was fully old
enough now to be apprenticed to Joe; and when Joe sat with the poker on
his knees thoughtfully raking out the ashes between the lower bars, my
sister would so distinctly construe that innocent action into
opposition on his part, that she would dive at him, take the poker out
of his hands, shake him, and put it away. There was a most irritating
end to every one of these debates. All in a moment, with nothing to
lead up to it, my sister would stop herself in a yawn, and catching
sight of me as it were incidentally, would swoop upon me with, “Come!
there’s enough of _you_! _You_ get along to bed; _you_’ve given trouble
enough for one night, I hope!” As if I had besought them as a favour to
bother my life out.

We went on in this way for a long time, and it seemed likely that we
should continue to go on in this way for a long time, when one day Miss
Havisham stopped short as she and I were walking, she leaning on my
shoulder; and said with some displeasure,—

“You are growing tall, Pip!”

I thought it best to hint, through the medium of a meditative look,
that this might be occasioned by circumstances over which I had no
control.

She said no more at the time; but she presently stopped and looked at
me again; and presently again; and after that, looked frowning and
moody. On the next day of my attendance, when our usual exercise was
over, and I had landed her at her dressing-table, she stayed me with a
movement of her impatient fingers:—

“Tell me the name again of that blacksmith of yours.”

“Joe Gargery, ma’am.”

“Meaning the master you were to be apprenticed to?”

“Yes, Miss Havisham.”

“You had better be apprenticed at once. Would Gargery come here with
you, and bring your indentures, do you think?”

I signified that I had no doubt he would take it as an honour to be
asked.

“Then let him come.”

“At any particular time, Miss Havisham?”

“There, there! I know nothing about times. Let him come soon, and come
along with you.”

When I got home at night, and delivered this message for Joe, my sister
“went on the Rampage,” in a more alarming degree than at any previous
period. She asked me and Joe whether we supposed she was door-mats
under our feet, and how we dared to use her so, and what company we
graciously thought she _was_ fit for?

He lodged at a sluice-keeper’s out on the marshes,
and on working-days would come slouching from his hermitage, with his
hands in his pockets and his dinner loosely tied in a bundle round his
neck and dangling on his back. On Sundays he mostly lay all day on the
sluice-gates, or stood against ricks and barns. He always slouched,
locomotively, with his eyes on the ground; and, when accosted or
otherwise required to raise them, he looked up in a half-resentful,
half-puzzled way, as though the only thought he ever had was, that it
was rather an odd and injurious fact that he should never be thinking.

This morose journeyman had no liking for me. When I was very small and
timid, he gave me to understand that the Devil lived in a black corner
of the forge, and that he knew the fiend very well: also that it was
necessary to make up the fire, once in seven years, with a live boy,
and that I might consider myself fuel. When I became Joe’s ’prentice,
Orlick was perhaps confirmed in some suspicion that I should displace
him; howbeit, he liked me still less. Not that he ever said anything,
or did anything, openly importing hostility; I only noticed that he
always beat his sparks in my direction, and that whenever I sang Old
Clem, he came in out of time.

Dolge Orlick was at work and present, next day, when I reminded Joe of
my half-holiday. He said nothing at the moment, for he and Joe had just
got a piece of hot iron between them, and I was at the bellows; but by
and by he said, leaning on his hammer,—

“Now, master! Sure you’re not a-going to favour only one of us. If
Young Pip has a half-holiday, do as much for Old Orlick.” I suppose he
was about five-and-twenty, but he usually spoke of himself as an
ancient person.

“Why, what’ll you do with a half-holiday, if you get it?” said Joe.

“What’ll _I_ do with it! What’ll _he_ do with it? I’ll do as much with
it as _him_,” said Orlick.

“As to Pip, he’s going up town,” said Joe.

“Well then, as to Old Orlick, _he_’s a-going up town,” retorted that
worthy. “Two can go up town. Tain’t only one wot can go up town.

“Don’t lose your temper,” said Joe.

“Shall if I like,” growled Orlick. “Some and their uptowning! Now,
master! Come. No favouring in this shop. Be a man!”

The master refusing to entertain the subject until the journeyman was
in a better temper, Orlick plunged at the furnace, drew out a red-hot
bar, made at me with it as if he were going to run it through my body,
whisked it round my head, laid it on the anvil, hammered it out,—as if
it were I, I thought, and the sparks were my spirting blood,—and
finally said, when he had hammered himself hot and the iron cold, and
he again leaned on his hammer,—

“Now, master!”

“Are you all right now?” demanded Joe.

“Ah! I am all right,” said gruff Old Orlick.

“Then, as in general you stick to your work as well as most men,” said
Joe, “let it be a half-holiday for all.”

My sister had been standing silent in the yard, within hearing,—she was
a most unscrupulous spy and listener,—and she instantly looked in at
one of the windows.

“Biddy,” said I, after binding her to secrecy, “I want to be a
gentleman.”

“O, I wouldn’t, if I was you!” she returned. “I don’t think it would
answer.”

“Biddy,” said I, with some severity, “I have particular reasons for
wanting to be a gentleman.”

“You know best, Pip; but don’t you think you are happier as you are?”

“Biddy,” I exclaimed, impatiently, “I am not at all happy as I am. I am
disgusted with my calling and with my life. I have never taken to
either, since I was bound. Don’t be absurd.”

“Was I absurd?” said Biddy, quietly raising her eyebrows; “I am sorry
for that; I didn’t mean to be. I only want you to do well, and to be
comfortable.”

“Well, then, understand once for all that I never shall or can be
comfortable—or anything but miserable—there, Biddy!—unless I can lead a
very different sort of life from the life I lead now.”

“That’s a pity!” said Biddy, shaking her head with a sorrowful air.

Now, I too had so often thought it a pity, that, in the singular kind
of quarrel with myself which I was always carrying on, I was half
inclined to shed tears of vexation and distress when Biddy gave
utterance to her sentiment and my own. I told her she was right, and I
knew it was much to be regretted, but still it was not to be helped.

“If I could have settled down,” I said to Biddy, plucking up the short
grass within reach, much as I had once upon a time pulled my feelings
out of my hair and kicked them into the brewery wall,—“if I could have
settled down and been but half as fond of the forge as I was when I was
little, I know it would have been much better for me. You and I and Joe
