humanity treats its gods. They worship us, and are always bothering us
to do something for them.”

“I should have said that whatever they ask for they had first given to
us,” murmured the lad gravely. “They create love in our natures. They
have a right to demand it back.”

“That is quite true, Dorian,” cried Hallward.

“Nothing is ever quite true,” said Lord Henry.

“This is,” interrupted Dorian. “You must admit, Harry, that women give
to men the very gold of their lives.”

“Possibly,” he sighed, “but they invariably want it back in such very
small change. That is the worry. Women, as some witty Frenchman once
put it, inspire us with the desire to do masterpieces and always
prevent us from carrying them out.”

“Harry, you are dreadful! I don’t know why I like you so much.”

“I am awfully sorry that I have made you waste an
evening, Harry. I apologize to you both.”

“My dear Dorian, I should think Miss Vane was ill,” interrupted
Hallward. “We will come some other night.”

“I wish she were ill,” he rejoined. “But she seems to me to be simply

artist. This evening she is merely a commonplace mediocre actress.”

“Don’t talk like that about any one you love, Dorian. Love is a more
wonderful thing than art.”

“They are both simply forms of imitation,” remarked Lord Henry. “But do
let us go. Dorian, you must not stay here any longer. It is not good

want your wife to act, so what does it matter if she plays Juliet like
a wooden doll? She is very lovely, and if she knows as little about
life as she does about acting, she will be a delightful experience.
There are only two kinds of people who are really fascinating—people
who know absolutely everything, and people who know absolutely nothing.
Good heavens, my dear boy, don’t look so tragic! The secret of
remaining young is never to have an emotion that is unbecoming. Come to
the club with Basil and myself. We will smoke cigarettes and drink to
the beauty of Sibyl Vane. She is beautiful. What more can you want?”

“Go away, Harry,” cried the lad. “I want to be alone. Basil, you must

leaned up against the wall, hiding his face in his hands.

“Let us go, Basil,” said Lord Henry with a strange tenderness in his
voice, and the two young men passed out together.

A few moments afterwards the footlights flared up and the curtain rose
on the third act. Dorian Gray went back to his seat. He looked pale,
and proud, and indifferent. The play dragged on, and seemed
interminable. Half of the audience went out, tramping in heavy boots
and laughing. The whole thing was a _fiasco_. The last act was played
to almost empty benches. The curtain went down on a titter and some
groans.

As soon as it was over, Dorian Gray rushed behind the scenes into the
greenroom. The girl was standing there alone, with a look of triumph on
her face. Her eyes were lit with an exquisite fire. There was a
radiance about her. Her parted lips were smiling over some secret of
their own.

When he entered, she looked at him, and an expression of infinite joy
came over her. “How badly I acted to-night, Dorian!” she cried.

“Horribly!” he answered, gazing at her in amazement. “Horribly! It was
dreadful. Are you ill? You have no idea what it was. You have no idea
what I suffered.”

The girl smiled. “Dorian,” she answered, lingering over his name with
long-drawn music in her voice, as though it were sweeter than honey to
the red petals of her mouth. “Dorian, you should have understood. But
you understand now, don’t you?”

“Understand what?” he asked, angrily.

“Why I was so bad to-night.

The picture had not changed. It was folly to think so.

Yet it was watching him, with its beautiful marred face and its cruel
smile. Its bright hair gleamed in the early sunlight. Its blue eyes met
his own. A sense of infinite pity, not for himself, but for the painted
image of himself, came over him. It had altered already, and would
alter more. Its gold would wither into grey. Its red and white roses
would die. For every sin that he committed, a stain would fleck and
wreck its fairness. But he would not sin. The picture, changed or
unchanged, would be to him the visible emblem of conscience. He would
resist temptation. He would not see Lord Henry any more—would not, at
any rate, listen to those subtle poisonous theories that in Basil
Hallward’s garden had first stirred within him the passion for
impossible things. He would go back to Sibyl Vane, make her amends,
marry her, try to love her again. Yes, it was his duty to do so. She
must have suffered more than he had. Poor child! He had been selfish
and cruel to her. The fascination that she had exercised over him would
return. They would be happy together. His life with her would be
beautiful and pure.

He got up from his chair and drew a large screen right in front of the
portrait, shuddering as he glanced at it. “How horrible!” he murmured

stepped out on to the grass, he drew a deep breath. The fresh morning

Sibyl. A faint echo of his love came back to him. He repeated her name
over and over again. The birds that were singing in the dew-drenched
garden seemed to be telling the flowers about her.


CHAPTER VIII.


It was long past noon when he awoke. His valet had crept several times
on tiptoe into the room to see if he was stirring, and had wondered
what made his young master sleep so late. Finally his bell sounded, and
Victor came in softly with a cup of tea, and a pile of letters, on a
small tray of old Sevres china, and drew back the olive-satin curtains,
with their shimmering blue lining, that hung in front of the three tall
windows.

“Monsieur has well slept this morning,” he said, smiling.

“What o’clock is it, Victor?” asked Dorian Gray drowsily.

“One hour and a quarter, Monsieur.”

How late it was! He sat up, and having sipped some tea, turned over his
letters. One of them was from Lord Henry, and had been brought by hand
that morning. He hesitated for a moment, and then put it aside. The
others he opened listlessly. They contained the usual collection of
cards, invitations to dinner, tickets for private views, programmes of
charity concerts, and the like that are showered on fashionable young
men every morning during the season. There was a rather heavy bill for

people and did not realize that we live in an age when unnecessary
things are our only necessities; and there were several very
courteously worded communications from Jermyn Street money-lenders

most reasonable rates of interest.

Things like that make a man fashionable in Paris.
But in London people are so prejudiced. Here, one should never make
one’s _début_ with a scandal. One should reserve that to give an
interest to one’s old age. I suppose they don’t know your name at the

round to her room? That is an important point.”

Dorian did not answer for a few moments. He was dazed with horror.
Finally he stammered, in a stifled voice, “Harry, did you say an

“I have no doubt it was not an accident, Dorian, though it must be put

“Harry, Harry, it is terrible!” cried the lad.

“Yes; it is very tragic, of course, but you must not get yourself mixed

“So I have murdered Sibyl Vane,” said Dorian Gray, half to himself,

Yet the roses are not less lovely for all that. The birds sing just as

extraordinarily dramatic life is! If I had read all this in a book,
Harry, I think I would have wept over it. Somehow, now that it has
happened actually, and to me, it seems far too wonderful for tears.
Here is the first passionate love-letter I have ever written in my
life. Strange, that my first passionate love-letter should have been

The moment she touched actual
life, she marred it, and it marred her, and so she passed away. Mourn

strangled. Cry out against Heaven because the daughter of Brabantio

There was a silence. The evening darkened in the room. Noiselessly, and

After some time Dorian Gray looked up. “You have explained me to

I wonder if life has still in store for me anything as marvellous.”

“Life has everything in store for you, Dorian. There is nothing that

“But suppose, Harry, I became haggard, and old, and wrinkled? What

“I think I shall join you at the opera, Harry. I feel too tired to eat

“We are only at the beginning of our friendship, Dorian,” answered Lord

As he closed the door behind him, Dorian Gray touched the bell, and in

She was always a heroine. The last night she played—the

The painter felt strangely moved. The lad was infinitely dear to him,

And yet the thing would still
live on. It would be always alive.

He shuddered, and for a moment he regretted that he had not told Basil

He took up from the couch the great purple-and-gold texture that

He passed out as his servant entered.

“The persons are here, Monsieur.”

He felt that the man must be got rid of at once. He must not be allowed

“Wait for an answer,” he said, handing it to him, “and show the men in

In two or three minutes there was another knock, and Mr. Hubbard

“What can I do for you, Mr. Gray?” he said, rubbing his fat freckled

sale.

What had Dorian Gray to do with Sibyl Vane’s death?
There was nothing to fear. Dorian Gray had not killed her.

His eye fell on the yellow book that Lord Henry had sent him. What was

It was a novel without a plot and with only one character, being,
indeed, simply a psychological study of a certain young Parisian who

produced in the mind of the lad, as he passed from chapter to chapter,

Cloudless, and pierced by one solitary star, a copper-green sky gleamed

It was almost nine o’clock before he reached the club, where he found

“Yes, I thought you would like it,” replied his host, rising from his

Gradually white fingers creep through the
curtains, and they appear to tremble. In black fantastic shapes, dumb

feared to wake the sleepers and yet must needs call forth sleep from

Nothing seems to us changed. Out of the unreal shadows of the night

It was the creation of such worlds as these that seemed to Dorian Gray

It was rumoured of him once that he was about to join the Roman

Even to read of the luxury of the dead was wonderful.

Then he turned his attention to embroideries and to the tapestries that

I hurried along here as fast as I could, and had just crossed a ditch I knew was close to the Battery, and had just climbed up the bank beyond it, when I spotted the man sitting in front of me. His back was to me, and his arms were crossed, and he was nodding forward, weighed down by sleep.

I thought he would be more pleased if I surprised him with his breakfast, so I crept forward and gently touched his shoulder. He immediately jumped up, but it was not the same man, but a different one!

And yet this man was also dressed in coarse grey, had a heavy iron on his leg, was limping, hoarse, and cold, and shared all the other traits of the first man; except for his face, and he wore a flat, wide-brimmed, low-crowned felt hat. I saw all this in an instant, for I had only a moment to take it in: he cursed at me, swung at me—it was a feeble round blow that missed me and nearly knocked himself over, for it made him stumble—and then he ran into the fog, stumbling twice as he went, and I lost sight of him.

'It’s the young man!' I thought, my heart leaping as I recognized him. I suppose I would have felt a pain in my liver too, if I had known where it was.

I soon reached the Battery after that, and there was the correct man—hugging himself and limping back and forth, as if he had never stopped hugging and limping all night—waiting for me. He was dreadfully cold, to be sure. I half expected to see him collapse before my eyes and die from the bitter cold. His eyes looked so dreadfully hungry too, that when I gave him the file and he placed it on the grass, it occurred to me he might have tried to eat it, if he had not noticed my bundle. He did not turn me upside down this time to get at what I had, but left me upright while I opened the bundle and emptied my pockets.

'What's in the bottle, boy?' he asked.

'Brandy,' I replied.

He was already shoving mincemeat down his throat in the most peculiar way—more like a man trying to store it away somewhere in a great rush, than a man eating it—but he paused to take some of the drink. He shivered so violently all the while, that it was quite a struggle for him to keep the bottle's neck between his teeth, without biting it off.

'I think you have the ague,' I said.

'I agree with you, boy,' he said.

'It’s bad in this place,' I told him. 'You’ve been lying out on the meshes, and they’re dreadful for causing ague. They’re rheumatic too.'

'I’ll eat my breakfast before they kill me,' he said. 'I would, even if I was going to be hanged on that gallows over there directly afterwards. I’ll beat the shivers so far, I’ll bet you.'

He was devouring mincemeat, meatbone, bread, cheese, and pork pie, all at once: staring suspiciously while he did so at the mist all around us, and often stopping—even pausing his chewing—to listen.

I bent over Joe and, using my finger, traced the letter for him to read.

'Extraordinary!' Joe exclaimed when I had finished. 'You really are a scholar.'

'How would you spell Gargery, Joe?' I asked, with a touch of condescending kindness.

'I don't spell it at all,' Joe replied.

'But if you did?'

'It can't be imagined,' said Joe. 'Though I do enjoy reading quite a bit myself.'

'Do you, Joe?'

'On-common. Give me,' said Joe, 'a fine book or a decent newspaper, and place me by a warm fire, and I could ask for nothing more. Lord!' he added, after rubbing his knees a bit, 'when you finally come across a J and an O, and say to yourself, 'Here at last is a J-O, Joe,' how fascinating reading becomes!'

From this, I gathered that Joe's education, like steam, was still in its early stages. Continuing the conversation, I asked:

'Did you never attend school, Joe, when you were as young as me?'

'No, Pip.'

'Why didn't you ever go to school, Joe, when you were as young as me?'

'Well, Pip,' said Joe, picking up the poker and settling into his usual thoughtful habit of slowly raking the fire between the lower bars; 'I'll tell you. My father, Pip, he had a tendency to drink, and when he was overcome by it, he would beat my mother cruelly. It was nearly the only beating he gave, indeed, except for the one he gave me. When evaluating an author's worth and determining their place among the literary pantheon, we are justified in assessing them from our own perspective and according to our own criteria. Yet, when considering the strength of their work, we must take into account their original intent and compare their creations to the vision they themselves set forth, measuring how much falls short. We differ from Mr. Poe in our views on the aims of art. He believes the goal is the creation of Beauty, and it may be only in the interpretation of that term that we find ourselves at odds. In our remarks on his writings, however, we shall follow his own standard as our guide. The sanctuary of the muse is open from every direction, and there is ample space within it for all who offer tribute or seek prophecy.

In his stories, Mr. Poe has chosen to demonstrate his talent primarily in that shadowy realm that lies at the edge of the plausible and stretches into the strange boundaries of superstition and the unreal. He possesses a striking ability to blend two faculties rarely found together: the capacity to affect the reader's mind with the subtle suggestions of mystery and an attention to detail so thorough that not even a pin or a button escapes notice. Both traits stem naturally from the dominant feature of his intellect, which we have previously mentioned—analysis. This is what sets the artist apart. His mind immediately grasps the desired effect. Once he has decided to evoke certain feelings in the reader, he ensures that every element contributes precisely to the central aim. Even his mystery is calculated in his mind. To him, X is a known variable throughout. In any scene he creates, he understands the chemical nature of all his colors. Although some of his figures may appear indistinct, and the shadows formless, to him the contours are as clear and defined as those of a geometric figure. For this reason, Mr. Poe has no affinity for Mysticism. The Mystic lives within the mystery, is wrapped in it; it tinges all his thoughts; it especially affects his vision, and the most ordinary things acquire a prismatic glow from it. Mr. Poe, by contrast, is an observer from the outside. He examines, he dissects, he watches

“with an eye serene,
The very pulse of the machine,”

for it is essentially a machine to him, with gears and cogs and piston-rods, all working to achieve a specific outcome.

This analytical nature of his mind tempers the poetic, and by giving him the endurance to be meticulous, allows him to inject a remarkable sense of reality into his most fantastical ideas. A monomania he portrays with great strength. He enjoys dissecting one of these mental tumors and tracing all the delicate extensions of its roots. In conjuring images of horror, too, he achieves unusual success, sometimes conveying to us by a faint suggestion some dreadful uncertainty, which is the essence of all horror. He leaves the imagination the task of completing the picture, a task to which only it is suited.

“For much imaginary work was there;
Conceit deceitful, so compact, so kind,
That for Achilles’ image stood his spear
Grasped in an armed hand; himself behind
Was left unseen, save to the eye of mind.”

In his stories, Mr. Poe primarily showcases his skills in that shadowy area that lies between the edges of the plausible and the strange world of superstition and fantasy. He uniquely blends two abilities that rarely go together: the power to affect the reader with the subtle hints of mystery and an attention to detail so thorough that not even a pin or a button is overlooked. Both stem from the dominant trait of his mind, which we've already mentioned—analysis. This is what sets the artist apart. His mind immediately focuses on the desired impact. Once he decides on the emotions he wants to evoke in the reader, he ensures every part of the work contributes directly to that goal. Even his mystery is logical to him. For him, X is a known variable throughout. In any scene he creates, he understands the chemical properties of all his colors. Although some of his figures might appear vague or shadowy, to him the outlines are as clear and defined as a geometric drawing. Because of this, Mr. Poe doesn't connect with Mysticism. The Mystic lives in the mystery, is surrounded by it; it influences all his thoughts; it especially affects his vision, and even ordinary things seem to have a rainbow-like glow. Mr. Poe, however, is an observer from the outside. He analyzes, he examines, he watches

“with an eye serene,
 The very pulse of the machine,”
which is how he sees it practically, with gears and cogs and piston rods, all working together to achieve a specific result.

This analytical side of his mind balances the poetic, and by giving him the patience to be detailed, it allows him to add a remarkable realism to his most unrealistic ideas. He portrays a monomania with great strength. He enjoys dissecting one of these mental disorders and tracing all the subtle connections of its roots. In creating images of horror, he also achieves unusual success, sometimes conveying to us through a dark suggestion some terrible uncertainty, which is the essence of all horror. He leaves it to the imagination to complete the picture, a task only imagination can handle.

“For much imaginary work was there;
 Conceit deceitful, so compact, so kind,
 That for Achilles’ image stood his spear
 Grasped in an armed hand; himself behind
 Was left unseen, save to the eye of mind.”

My overall goal is to launch a Magazine named 'The Stylus,' but it would serve no purpose for me, even after it is launched, unless it is entirely beyond the reach of a publisher. Therefore, I intend to create a publication that is wholly under my own control. To achieve this, I need a list of at least five hundred subscribers to begin with; I already have nearly two hundred. I plan to travel South and West to visit my personal and literary acquaintances—former college and West Point friends—to gauge what I can accomplish. To secure the funds needed to take the first step, I intend to deliver a lecture at the Society Library on Thursday, the 3rd of February, and to avoid any potential for disagreement, my topic will not be literary in nature. I have selected a broad theme: 'The Universe.'

Having thus shared the facts of the matter, I leave the rest to your own discretion and kindness. With deep gratitude, most deeply grateful,

Your friend always,
EDGAR A. POE.

Though brief and hastily written, these letters clearly demonstrate the very traits that have been denied to Mr. Poe—humility, determination, trust in the friendship of others, and the ability to form warm and appreciative friendships! This was assuredly the case when he was in his right mind. This is the only impression he has consistently made on us during our acquaintance of five or six years. It is far simpler to believe what we have witnessed and experienced than to accept what we have only heard, and so we remember him with admiration and respect; these accounts of him in a state of moral disorder seem to us like portraits painted during illness of a man we have only known in health.

There is another, more touching and far more compelling proof of Edgar A. Poe's goodness. To reveal it, we must risk unveiling the veil that respectfully shrouds grief and refinement in poverty; but we believe it may be justified if we can enhance the poet's memory, even if there were not a more urgent and necessary service it might provide to the closest link severed by his death.

Our first knowledge of Mr. Poe's relocation to this city came through a visit we received from a lady who introduced herself to us as the mother of his wife. She was seeking employment for him, and she explained her request by stating that he was unwell, that her daughter was a chronic invalid, and that their situation was so dire that she had taken it upon herself. The lady's countenance, made radiant and angelic by her evident total sacrifice of her life to hardship and sorrowful care, her gentle and sorrowful voice pleading her case, her long-forgotten but habitual and unconscious refinement, and her appealing yet appreciative references to the merits and talents of her son, immediately revealed the presence of one of those angels on earth that women in adversity can become. It was a difficult fate she was watching over. Mr. Poe wrote with great difficulty and in a style too elevated for the general public to appreciate, and thus he was poorly compensated.

After nearly four and a half hours, I determined the balloon was sufficiently inflated. I then fastened the car and placed all my tools inside, making sure to include the condensing equipment, a plentiful supply of water, and ample provisions, such as pemmican, which offers substantial nourishment in a compact form. I also brought along a pair of pigeons and a cat. It was now almost dawn, and I felt it was time to leave. Pretending to drop a lit cigar, I used the moment to crouch and quietly set fire to the slow match, the end of which slightly extended beyond the rim of one of the smaller barrels. The three men who had been pestering me noticed nothing of this. I jumped into the car and severed the single rope tethering me to the ground, delighted to see that I rose easily, carrying one hundred and seventy-five pounds of lead ballast, with the capacity to lift as much more.

“Yet scarcely had I reached fifty yards in height when a terrible storm of fire, smoke, sulfur, limbs, gravel, burning wood, and glowing metal surged upward after me in a most dreadful and chaotic fashion. My heart sank, and I fell to the bottom of the car, shaking with sheer terror. At that moment, I realized I had overestimated the situation, and the full impact of the blast was yet to come. Almost immediately, I felt a rush of blood to my temples, followed by a jarring shock that I shall never forget, which tore through the night and seemed to split the very heavens. Later, I was able to understand that the intensity of the explosion on me was due to my position directly above it, in the path of its greatest force. But at the time, I was only concerned with saving my life. The balloon first collapsed, then violently expanded, then spun wildly at a terrifying speed, and finally, swaying and lurching like a drunkard, it hurled me over the edge of the car with great force, leaving me hanging at a terrifying height, head down and face outward, by a slender cord about three feet long, which had accidentally caught through a crack in the wicker and entangled my left foot as I fell. It is impossible—utterly impossible—to imagine the horror of my condition. I gasped for breath convulsively, a shudder like a fit of the ague shook every nerve and muscle in my body, my eyes seemed to pop from their sockets, a terrible nausea overwhelmed me—and finally, I lost consciousness.

“How long I remained in this state is unknown. It must have been a considerable time, for when I regained some sense of being, I found the dawn breaking, the balloon at an immense height above an endless expanse of ocean, and no sign of land anywhere within the vast horizon.

But once I completed it, I quickly began to benefit from my invention. I could breathe freely and easily again—and why not? I was also pleasantly surprised to find that I was mostly free from the severe pain that had been troubling me. I now only had a mild headache, along with a feeling of fullness or tightness in my wrists, ankles, and throat. It was clear that most of the discomfort from removing atmospheric pressure had worn off, as I had expected, and much of the pain I had endured for the past two hours could be blamed entirely on poor breathing.

At twenty minutes before nine o’clock—that is, shortly before I sealed the chamber—the mercury in the barometer reached its lowest point. As I mentioned earlier, this was a special type of barometer. It showed that I had reached an altitude of 132,000 feet, or about twenty-five miles. At that time, I could see a vast portion of the Earth’s surface—about one three-hundred-and-twentieth of the whole. By nine o’clock, I had lost sight of land to the east, but not before I noticed that the balloon was moving quickly in a north-northwest direction. The curvature of the ocean below was clearly visible, although my view was often blocked by clouds drifting around.

'April 5th. I witnessed the unusual sight of the sun rising while nearly the entire visible surface of the earth remained in darkness. Eventually, the light spread fully, and I once more saw the line of ice to the north. It was now very clear and appeared much darker than the ocean. I was clearly approaching it quickly. I thought I could again spot a strip of land to the east and one to the west, but I could not be certain. The weather was mild. Nothing of consequence happened during the day. I went to bed early.

'April 6th. I was astonished to find the ice rim at a short distance, with a vast expanse of the same material stretching far into the horizon to the north. It was obvious that if the balloon kept its current path, it would soon reach the Frozen Ocean, and I had little doubt I would eventually see the Pole. Throughout the day, I continued to draw closer to the ice. As night approached, the limits of my horizon suddenly expanded significantly, likely due to the earth's shape being an oblate spheroid and my reaching the flattened areas near the Arctic circle. When darkness finally came, I went to bed with great concern, fearing I might pass over the object of so much curiosity without a chance to observe it.

'April 7th. I awoke early, and to my great delight, finally saw what could only be the northern Pole itself. It was there, without a doubt, directly beneath my feet; but alas, I had now risen so high that nothing could be clearly discerned. In fact, judging from the progression of numbers showing my altitudes at different times between six A.M. on the second of April and twenty minutes before nine A.M. of the same day (when the barometer dropped), it could be reasonably inferred that the balloon had reached a height of no less than 7,254 miles above sea level by four o'clock in the morning of April the seventh. This elevation may seem immense, but the estimate was likely much lower than the actual height. At any rate, I certainly saw the entire earth's major diameter; the whole northern hemisphere lay beneath me like an orthographic projection: and the great circle of the equator itself formed the boundary of my horizon. You may, however, easily imagine that the unexplored regions within the Arctic circle, though directly beneath me and seen without any foreshortening, were still relatively too small and at too great a distance from the point of view to allow for any very accurate examination.

I have much to say about the climate of the planet; its remarkable shifts between heat and cold, with scorching sunshine for one fortnight and more than polar chill for the next; a continuous movement of moisture, like distillation in a vacuum, from the spot beneath the sun to the spot farthest from it; a shifting zone of flowing water; the people themselves; their customs, manners, and political systems; their unique physical structure; their ugliness; their lack of ears, those useless appendages in such an altered atmosphere; their ignorance of the use and nature of speech due to this; their alternative means of communication through a strange method; the inexplicable link between each individual on the moon and a specific individual on the earth—a connection similar to, and based upon, that of the planet's orbs and satellites, through which the fates of the inhabitants of one are entwined with those of the other; and above all, if it pleases your Excellencies—above all, of those dark and terrible secrets hidden in the distant parts of the moon—regions that, due to the almost miraculous alignment of the satellite’s rotation on its axis with its sidereal revolution around the earth, have never yet been turned, and, by God’s grace, never shall be turned, to the scrutiny of human telescopes. All this, and much more—far more—would I gladly explain. But, to be brief, I must have my reward. I long for a return to my family and my home; and as the price for any further information I can offer—in exchange for the insight I can provide on many significant aspects of physical and metaphysical science—I must request, through your esteemed body’s influence, a pardon for the crime I committed in the death of the creditors upon my departure from Rotterdam. This, then, is the purpose of this letter. Its bearer, an inhabitant of the moon, whom I have convinced and properly instructed to serve as my messenger to the earth, will await your Excellencies’ decision and return to me with the pardon in question, if it can in any way be secured. Upon arriving at the hut, I knocked as was my habit, and receiving no answer, I searched for the key in the spot I knew it was hidden, unlocked the door, and stepped inside. A pleasant fire was burning in the fireplace. It was a welcome sight, and I was glad to see it. I removed my coat, took a chair by the crackling logs, and waited calmly for my hosts to arrive.

Soon after nightfall they came, greeting me with great warmth. Jupiter, beaming with delight, bustled around preparing some marsh hens for supper. Legrand was in one of his fits—how else can I describe them?—of excitement. He had discovered an unfamiliar bivalve, which he believed formed a new genus, and more than that, he had tracked down and captured, with Jupiter’s help, a _scarabæus_ that he thought might be entirely new, though he wanted my opinion on the matter the next day.

“And why not tonight?” I asked, rubbing my hands by the fire, wishing the whole tribe of _scarabæi_ were far away.

“Ah, if only I had known you were here!” Legrand replied. “It’s been so long since I last saw you, and how could I have imagined you would visit on this very night of all nights? On my way home I met Lieutenant G—— from the fort, and, foolishly, I lent him the bug. So you won’t be able to see it until morning. Stay here tonight, and I’ll send Jup to fetch it at sunrise. It is the most beautiful thing in existence!”

“What?—sunrise?”

“Nonsense! No!—the bug. It is a brilliant gold color—about the size of a large hickory-nut—with two jet black spots near one end of the back, and another, a bit longer, at the other. The _antennæ_ are—”

“Dey ain’t no tin in him, Massa Will, I keep a tellin on you,” Jupiter interjected. “De bug is a goole bug, solid, ebery bit of him, inside and all, sep him wing—neber feel half so hebby a bug in my life.”

“Well, suppose it is, Jup,” Legrand replied, with more urgency than the situation seemed to require, “is that any reason for you to let the birds burn? The color”—he turned to me—“is really almost enough to support Jupiter’s idea. You have never seen a more brilliant metallic sheen than the scales emit—but you cannot judge that until tomorrow. In the meantime, I can give you some idea of the shape.” With that, he sat down at a small table where a pen and ink were placed, but there was no paper. He searched a drawer for some, but found none.

“Never mind,” he said at last, “this will do.” And from his waistcoat pocket he pulled out a scrap of what I assumed to be very dirty foolscap, and sketched a rough drawing with the pen. While he did this, I remained seated by the fire, still feeling the chill. When the sketch was finished, he handed it to me without getting up. As I took it, a loud growl was heard, followed by scratching at the door. Jupiter opened it, and a large Newfoundland belonging to Legrand came in, leaping onto my shoulders and showering me with affection; for I had shown him much attention during my previous visits.

I feared that the unrelenting weight of misfortune had finally driven my friend to the edge of reason. Without a moment's delay, I decided to accompany the negro.

When we arrived at the dock, I observed a scythe and three spades, all brand new, resting at the bottom of the boat we were to use.

“What is the purpose of these, Jup?” I asked.

“Him syfe, massa, and spade.”

“Indeed; but why are they here?”

“Him de syfe and de spade what Massa Will told me to buy for him in town, and it cost me a fortune to get ’em.”

“But what, in the name of all that is strange, is your ‘Massa Will’ going to do with scythes and spades?”

“That’s more than I know, and the devil take me if I don’t think it’s more than he knows too. But it’s all because of that bug.”

Since I could gain no clarity from Jupiter, whose mind seemed entirely consumed by 'de bug,' I stepped into the boat and we set sail. With a brisk wind at our backs, we quickly reached the small cove north of Fort Moultrie, and a two-mile walk brought us to the hut. It was about three in the afternoon when we arrived. Legrand had been waiting for us with great anticipation. He seized my hand with a nervous eagerness that unsettled me and reinforced my suspicions. His face was pale, almost deathly so, and his deep-set eyes gleamed with an unnatural brightness. After a few inquiries about his health, I asked him, not knowing what else to say, if he had yet obtained the _scarabæus_ from Lieutenant G——.

“Oh, yes,” he replied, his face flushing, “I got it from him the next morning. Nothing would tempt me to part with that _scarabæus_. Do you know that Jupiter is quite right about it?”

“In what way?” I asked, with a growing sense of unease.

“In thinking it is a bug made of _real gold_.” He spoke with such solemnity that I felt a deep sense of shock.

“This bug is going to make my fortune,” he continued, with a triumphant grin, “to restore me to my family’s estate. Is it any wonder, then, that I value it? Since Fortune has seen fit to give it to me, I only need to use it properly and I shall find the gold it points to. Jupiter; bring me that _scarabæus!_”

“What! de bug, massa? I’d rather not go fetch that bug for you—you must get him for yourself.” Legrand then rose with a solemn and dignified manner and retrieved the beetle from a glass case where it was kept. It was a beautiful scarabæus, and, at that time, unknown to naturalists—naturally a great treasure from a scientific standpoint. There were two round, black spots near one end of its back, and a long one near the other. The scales were incredibly hard and shiny, with the look of polished gold. The weight of the insect was remarkable, and, considering all these things, I could hardly fault Jupiter for his belief about it; but what to make of Legrand’s agreement with that belief, I could not, for the life of me, understand.

I apologize; I had overlooked the fact that Shakespeare will not emerge for seventeen hundred and fifty years yet. But does not the presence of Epidaphne support my calling it grotesque?

'It is well protected; and in this regard, it owes as much to nature as to human effort.'

That is quite accurate.

'There are an immense number of grand palaces.'

Indeed there are.

'And the many temples, rich and splendid, can rival the most celebrated of ancient times.'

I must admit all this. Still, there is an endless number of huts and wretched hovels. We cannot help but notice the filth in every gutter, and, were it not for the overpowering scent of idolatrous incense, I have no doubt we would detect a most unbearable stench. Have you ever seen streets so unbearably narrow, or houses so astonishingly tall? What gloom their shadows cast upon the ground! It is fortunate that the hanging lamps in those endless colonnades remain lit all day; otherwise, we would experience the darkness of Egypt in her time of ruin.

'It is certainly an odd place! What is the purpose of that peculiar structure? Look! It rises above all others, and lies to the east of what I believe to be the royal palace!'

That is the new Temple of the Sun, who is revered in Syria under the name Elah Gabalah. In the future, a very notorious Roman Emperor will establish this worship in Rome and thus gain a name, Heliogabalus. I daresay you would enjoy a glimpse of the temple's deity. You need not gaze upward at the sky; his Sunship is not there—at least not the Sunship venerated by the Syrians. That god will be found within that building. He is worshipped in the form of a large stone pillar ending at the top in a cone or pyramid, which signifies Fire.

'Listen—look!—who can those absurd figures be, half-naked, with their faces painted, shouting and gesturing to the crowd?'

Some are charlatans. Others belong more specifically to the class of philosophers. The majority, however—those who especially strike the crowd with clubs—are the chief courtiers of the palace, carrying out, as their duty, some commendable jest of the king's.

'But what do we have here? Good heavens! The town is teeming with wild animals! How dreadful a sight!—how perilous a feature!'

Dreadful, if you will; but in no way perilous. Each beast, if you will take the trouble to notice, is quietly following its master. A few, to be certain, are led by a rope around the neck, but these are mostly the smaller or timid kinds. The lion, the tiger, and the leopard are entirely unrestrained. They have been trained without difficulty to their current role, and accompany their respective owners as valets-de-chambre. It is true, there are moments when Nature reclaims her violated dominion;—but then the devouring of a soldier, or the choking of a sacred bull, is an event too trivial to be more than hinted at in Epidaphne.

'But what extraordinary commotion do I hear? Surely this is a loud noise even for Antioch! It suggests some disturbance of unusual interest.'

THE MURDERS IN THE RUE MORGUE

What melody the Syrens sang, or what name Achilles took when he disguised himself among women, though they are puzzling, are not entirely beyond guesswork.

—Sir Thomas Browne.

The mental traits described as analytical are, in themselves, not easily broken down. We understand them only through their effects. We know that for those who possess them in excess, they bring the greatest joy. Just as a strong man takes pride in his physical strength, enjoying tasks that test his muscles, so the analyst takes pride in the mental act of unraveling. He finds pleasure even in the smallest tasks that engage his abilities. He enjoys riddles, wordplay, and symbols; in solving them, he shows a level of sharpness that seems almost supernatural to most. His conclusions, achieved through the very core of method, truly resemble intuition.

The ability to break things down may be greatly strengthened by studying mathematics, especially its highest branch, which, unfairly and due to its backward process, has been labeled, as if by right, analysis. Yet calculation alone is not analysis. A chess player, for example, performs the former without effort toward the latter. It follows that the game of chess, in its impact on the mind, is often misunderstood. I am not composing a formal essay now, but merely introducing a somewhat unusual story with some random observations; I will therefore take the chance to claim that the higher functions of the reflective mind are more clearly and usefully tested by the modest game of checkers than by all the elaborate frivolity of chess. In chess, where the pieces move in different and strange ways, with varying and shifting values, what is merely complex is often mistaken (a common mistake) for what is deep. Here, attention is strongly engaged. If it wavers for a moment, a mistake is made, leading to loss or failure. The possible moves being not only numerous but intricate, the chances of such errors increase; and in nine out of ten cases, it is the more focused rather than the more clever player who wins. In checkers, on the other hand, where the moves are fixed and have little variation, the chances of error are reduced, and the mere attention is left relatively free, so that any advantage gained by either side comes from greater insight. To be more concrete, let us imagine a game of checkers where the pieces are limited to four kings, and where, of course, no mistake is expected. It is clear that here the outcome (with both players being equally skilled) can only be decided by some clever move, the result of a strong effort of the mind. Stripped of usual tools, the analyst enters the mindset of his opponent, aligns himself with it, and often sees, at a glance, the only methods (sometimes absurdly simple) by which he might lead the opponent into error or rush into a miscalculation.

No one now doubted that the mystery of this murder would soon be solved. Yet, despite a few arrests that initially seemed promising, nothing emerged that could connect the suspected individuals; they were released immediately. Surprisingly, three weeks had passed since the body was found, and no information had surfaced, and not even a whisper of the events that had stirred public concern had reached Dupin and me. Engrossed in our own investigations, we had not left our home or welcomed a visitor in nearly a month, nor had we paid much attention to the leading political pieces in the daily papers. The first news of the murder came from G—— himself. He visited us early on the afternoon of July 13th, 18—, and stayed with us until late into the night. He had grown frustrated by his inability to uncover the killers. His reputation, he claimed with a distinctly Parisian flair, was on the line. Even his honor was at stake. He ended a rather peculiar speech with praise for what he called Dupin’s keen sense, and made him a direct and generous offer, the exact nature of which I cannot reveal, as it is not relevant to my story.

My friend responded to the compliment as best he could, but accepted the offer immediately, even though its benefits were only temporary. Once this was settled, the Prefect began explaining his own theories, adding lengthy remarks on the evidence, which we had not yet seen. He spoke at length and with great learning, while I offered the occasional suggestion as the night slowly wore on. It was clearly shown that no such indifference existed; the elderly woman was extremely weak and so upset she could not manage any duties; St. Eustache, far from taking the news calmly, was overwhelmed with sorrow, and his behavior was so wild that M. Beauvais convinced a friend and relative to take care of him and stop him from attending the examination at the body’s removal. Furthermore, although L’Etoile claimed the corpse was reburied at public expense—that the family refused a generous offer for private sculpture—and that no family member attended the ceremony; yet all these claims were thoroughly disproven. In a later issue of the paper, an attempt was made to cast doubt on Beauvais himself. The editor wrote:

“Now, a shift occurs in the situation. We are told that on one occasion, while a Madame B—— was at Madame Rogêt’s home, M. Beauvais, who was leaving, told her that a gendarme was expected there, and that she, Madame B., must not speak to the gendarme until he returned, but leave the matter to him.... In the current state of affairs, M. Beauvais appears to have the whole matter locked in his mind. No step can be taken without M. Beauvais, for, go where you may, you meet him.... For some reason, he decided that no one else should handle the proceedings but himself, and he has pushed aside the male relatives in a peculiar manner, as they claim. He seems to have been strongly against allowing the relatives to view the body.”

Some support for the suspicion against Beauvais came from the following incident. A visitor to his office, a few days before the girl vanished, and while the occupant was away, noticed a rose in the keyhole of the door, and the name “Marie” written on a slate nearby.

We must remember that, generally speaking, newspapers aim more to provoke a reaction—to make a point—than to advance the cause of truth. The latter is only pursued when it aligns with the former. A publication that merely agrees with common opinion (however sound this opinion may be) gains no favor with the public. The majority of people consider profound only those who offer sharp contradictions to the prevailing thought. In reasoning, no less than in writing, it is the witty remark that is most quickly and widely appreciated. In both, it is the least commendable form of expression. 'What I mean to say is, that it is the blend of wit and drama in the idea—that Marie Rogêt is still alive—that has led L’Etoile to propose this theory, rather than any genuine likelihood of the idea. Let us consider the points of this journal’s argument, striving to avoid the confusion with which it is originally presented. 'The first goal of the writer is to demonstrate, based on the short time between Marie’s disappearance and the discovery of the floating body, that this body cannot be Marie’s. Reducing this time to its shortest possible length thus becomes the immediate aim of the thinker. In his hasty pursuit of this aim, he jumps to an assumption right away. 'It is foolish to believe,' he states, 'that the murder, if it occurred on her body, could have been completed quickly enough to allow her killers to cast the body into the river before midnight.' We instantly and naturally ask, why? Why is it foolish to believe the murder took place just five minutes after the girl left her mother’s home? Why is it foolish to believe it occurred at any given time of the day? There have been murders at all hours. But if the murder had occurred at any moment between nine in the morning on Sunday and a quarter before midnight, there would still have been enough time 'to cast the body into the river before midnight.' This assumption, then, amounts precisely to this—that the murder did not occur on Sunday at all—and, if we allow L’Etoile to make this assumption, we might as well allow it any liberties. The paragraph beginning 'It is foolish to believe that the murder, etc.,' as it appears in L’Etoile, may be imagined to have existed in the mind of its author thus—'It is foolish to believe that the murder, if it occurred on her body, could have been committed quickly enough to allow her killers to cast the body into the river before midnight; it is foolish, we say, to believe all this, and to believe at the same time, (as we are determined to believe,) that the body was not cast in until after midnight'—a sentence somewhat incoherent in itself, but not as absurd as the one actually printed. 'Were it my purpose,' continued Dupin, 'merely to _construct a case_ against this portion of L’Etoile’s argument, I might safely leave it as it is.'

Before daylight in the mornings I would sneak into cornfields and take a watermelon, or a mushmelon, or a punkin, or some fresh corn, or things like that. Pap always said it wasn’t any harm to borrow things if you meant to pay them back later; but the widow said it was just a soft name for stealing, and no decent person would do it. Jim said he thought the widow was partly right and pap was partly right; so the best way would be for us to pick out two or three things from the list and say we wouldn’t borrow them anymore—then he thought it wouldn’t be any harm to borrow the others. I was glad the way it turned out, too, because crabapples are never good, and the p’simmons wouldn’t be ripe for two or three months yet.

“Well, this is too many for me, Jim. I hain’t seen no fog, nor no islands, nor no troubles, nor nothing. I been setting here talking with you all night till you went to sleep about ten minutes ago, and I reckon I done the same. You couldn’t a got drunk in that time, so of course you’ve been dreaming.”

“Dad fetch it, how is I gwyne to dream all dat in ten minutes?”

“Well, hang it all, you did dream it, because there didn’t any of it happen.”

“But, Huck, it’s all jis’ as plain to me as—”

“It don’t make no difference how plain it is; there ain’t nothing in it. I know, because I’ve been here all the time.”

Jim didn’t say nothing for about five minutes, but set there studying over it. Then he says:

“Well, den, I reck’n I did dream it, Huck; but dog my cats ef it ain’t de powerfullest dream I ever see. En I hain’t ever had no dream b’fo’ dat’s tired me like dis one.”

“Oh, well, that’s all right, because a dream does tire a body like everything sometimes. But this one was a staving dream; tell me all about it, Jim.”

So Jim went to work and told me the whole thing right through, just as it happened, only he painted it up considerable. Then he said he must start in and “’terpret” it, because it was sent for a warning. He said the first tow-head stood for a man that would try to do us some good, but the current was another man that would get us away from him. The whoops was warnings that would come to us every now and then, and if we didn’t try hard to make out to understand them they’d just take us into bad luck, ’stead of keeping us out of it. The lot of tow-heads was troubles we was going to get into with quarrelsome people and all kinds of mean folks, but if we minded our business and didn’t talk back and aggravate them, we would pull through and get out of the fog and into the big clear river, which was the free States, and wouldn’t have no more trouble.

It had clouded up pretty dark just after I got on to the raft, but it was clearing up again now.

“Oh, well, that’s all interpreted well enough as far as it goes, Jim,” I says; “but what does _these_ things stand for?”

“Well, the fog—the fog that’s been around all night. The best place to find canoes is near rafts that are tied up along the shore. But we didn't see any rafts tied up, so we floated along for more than three hours. The night turned gray and thick, almost like fog. You can't see the river's shape or anything far away in weather like that. It got very late and quiet, and then a steamboat came up the river. We lit the lantern, hoping it would catch their attention. Boats going upstream usually stay far away from us; they follow the sandbars and look for smooth water near the rocks. But on nights like this, they push right up the middle of the river.

We could hear the boat rumbling along, but we couldn't see it clearly until it was almost on top of us. It was heading straight for us. They often do that, trying to see how close they can get without hitting anything. Sometimes the wheel cuts off a piece of the raft, and then the pilot sticks his head out and laughs, thinking he's clever. Well, here it came, and we thought it was going to try to pass us closely; but it didn't seem to be turning away at all. It was a big boat, and it was moving fast, too, looking like a black cloud with rows of glow-worms around it. Then suddenly it expanded, big and frightening, with a long line of open furnace doors glowing like red-hot teeth, and its huge bow and guards hanging right over us. There was a shout at us, and the sound of bells to stop the engines, a lot of swearing, and steam hissing—and as Jim jumped into the water on one side and I on the other, it smashed straight through the raft.

I dove—and I meant to reach the bottom, too, because a thirty-foot wheel was going to pass over me, and I wanted it to have plenty of space. I could usually stay underwater for a minute; this time I guess I stayed under for a minute and a half. Then I shot up to the surface quickly, because I was about to burst. I came up to my armpits and blew the water out of my nose, and caught my breath. Of course there was a strong current; and of course the boat started its engines again ten seconds after it stopped them, because they didn't care much for raftsmen; so now it was churning up the river, out of sight in the thick weather, though I could still hear it.

I called out for Jim about a dozen times, but I didn't get any answer; so I grabbed a plank that brushed against me while I was treading water, and swam for the shore, pushing the plank ahead of me. But I noticed that the current was pulling me toward the left-hand shore, which meant I was in a crossing; so I changed direction and swam that way.

There was one where a young lady was at a window gazing up at the moon, with tears sliding down her cheeks; she held an open letter in one hand, showing black sealing wax on one edge, and pressed a locket with a chain against her mouth. Underneath the picture it read, 'And Art Thou Gone Yes Thou Art Gone Alas.' These were all nice pictures, I suppose, but somehow they didn't sit well with me, because they always made me feel worse when I was already feeling down. Everyone was sorry she passed away, because she had planned to do many more of these pictures, and you could tell by the ones she had completed what she had lost. But I figured, given her nature, she was probably having a better time in the graveyard. She was working on what they said was her greatest picture when she fell ill, and every day and night she prayed to be allowed to live until she finished it, but she never got the chance. It was a picture of a young woman in a long white dress, standing on the rail of a bridge, ready to jump, with her hair flowing down her back, looking up at the moon, tears streaming down her face, with two arms folded across her chest, two arms stretched out in front, and two more reaching up toward the moon—and the idea was to see which pair looked best, then scratch out the others; but, as I was saying, she died before she could decide, and now they kept this picture over the head of the bed in her room, and every time her birthday came around, they hung flowers on it. Other times it was covered with a small curtain. The young woman in the picture had a kind of sweet, gentle face, but with so many arms, she seemed too spidery to me.

This young girl kept a scrapbook while she was alive, and used to paste obituaries, accidents, and cases of patient suffering from the _Presbyterian Observer_ into it, and then write poetry of her own after them. It was very good poetry. This is what she wrote about a boy named Stephen Dowling Bots who fell down a well and drowned:

ODE TO STEPHEN DOWLING BOTS, DEC’D

And did young Stephen sicken,
And did young Stephen die?
And did the sad hearts thicken,
And did the mourners cry?

No; such was not the fate of
Young Stephen Dowling Bots;
Though sad hearts round him thickened,
’Twas not from sickness’ shots.

No whooping-cough did rack his frame,
Nor measles drear with spots;
Not these impaired the sacred name
Of Stephen Dowling Bots.

Despised love struck not with woe
That head of curly knots,
Nor stomach troubles laid him low,
Young Stephen Dowling Bots.

O no. Then list with tearful eye,
Whilst I his fate do tell.
His soul did from this cold world fly
By falling down a well.

They got him out and emptied him;
Alas it was too late;
His spirit was gone for to sport aloft
In the realms of the good and great.

The next Sunday we all went to church, about three miles away, everyone riding horseback. The men brought their guns along, Buck did too, and they kept them between their knees or propped them against the wall. The Shepherdsons did the same. The preaching was pretty dull—it was all about brotherly love and other tiring topics; but everyone said it was a fine sermon, and they talked about it on the way home, having so much to say about faith and good works and free grace and predestination, and all sorts of other things, that it seemed to me to be one of the toughest Sundays I had ever come across.

About an hour after dinner, everyone was lounging around, some in their chairs and some in their rooms, and it got pretty boring. Buck and a dog were lying on the grass in the sun, fast asleep. I went up to our room and thought I’d take a nap myself. I found sweet Miss Sophia standing in her doorway, which was next to ours, and she led me into her room and closed the door gently, asking me if I liked her, and I said I did; and she asked me if I would do something for her and not tell anyone, and I said I would. Then she said she had forgotten her Testament and left it in the church pew between two other books, and would I sneak out quietly and go get it for her and not say a word to anyone. I said I would. So I slipped out and hurried up the road, and there wasn’t a soul at the church, except maybe a couple of hogs, for the door wasn’t locked, and hogs like a puncheon floor in summer because it’s cool. If you notice, most folks don’t go to church unless they have to; but a hog is different.

I told myself something was up; it wasn’t natural for a girl to be so worked up about a Testament. So I shook it, and out fell a little scrap of paper with “Half-past two” written on it with a pencil. I went through it, but couldn’t find anything else. I couldn’t make heads or tails of it, so I put the paper back in the book, and when I got home and upstairs, there was Miss Sophia in her doorway waiting for me. She pulled me in and shut the door; then she looked through the Testament till she found the paper, and as soon as she read it she looked happy; and before you could think she hugged me and said I was the best boy in the world and not to tell anyone. She was quite red in the face for a minute, and her eyes lit up, and it made her very pretty. I was quite surprised, but when I caught my breath I asked her what the paper was about, and she asked me if I had read it, and I said no, and she asked me if I could read writing, and I told her “no, only big letters,” and then she said the paper wasn’t anything but a book-mark to keep her place, and I might go and play now.

As soon as it was dark we pushed off; when we got her out to about the middle we let her go, and let her float wherever the current wanted her to; then we lit the pipes, and dangled our legs in the water, and talked about all sorts of things—we were always naked, day and night, whenever the mosquitoes would let us—the new clothes Buck’s folks made for me was too good to be comfortable, and besides I didn’t go much on clothes, nohow.

Sometimes we’d have that whole river all to ourselves for the longest time. Yonder was the banks and the islands, across the water; and maybe a spark—which was a candle in a cabin window; and sometimes on the water you could see a spark or two—on a raft or a scow, you know; and maybe you could hear a fiddle or a song coming over from one of them crafts. It’s lovely to live on a raft. We had the sky up there, all speckled with stars, and we used to lay on our backs and look up at them, and discuss about whether they was made or only just happened. Jim he allowed they was made, but I allowed they happened; I judged it would have took too long to make so many. 'No,' says the king.

'Easy!'

'All right. I’m just a-freezin’ for something fresh, anyway. Let’s commence right away.'

So the duke told him all about who Romeo was and who Juliet was, and said he was used to being Romeo, so the king could be Juliet.

'No, don’t you worry; these country jakes won’t ever think of that. All the idlers looked pleased; I figured they were used to getting amusement from Boggs. One of them said:

Another one said, “I wish old Boggs would threaten me, ’cause then I’d know I wasn’t going to die for a thousand years.”

Boggs came tearing along on his horse, whooping and yelling like an Indian, and shouting:

The whole party were but just reassembled in the drawing-room when Mr.

Mr. Weston meanwhile, perfectly unsuspicious of the indignation he was

She had no
doubt as to his being less in love—but neither his agitated spirits,

This was the only visit from Frank Churchill in the course of ten days.
He was often hoping, intending to come—but was always prevented. His

It soon appeared that London was not the place for her. She could not

Emma heard that Frank wrote in the highest spirits of this arrangement,
and seemed most fully to appreciate the blessing of having two months
before him of such near neighbourhood to many dear friends—for the
house was taken for May and June. She was told that now he wrote with
the greatest confidence of being often with them, almost as often as he
could even wish.

Emma saw how Mr. Weston understood these joyous prospects. He was
considering her as the source of all the happiness they offered. She
hoped it was not so. Two months must bring it to the proof.

Mr. Weston’s own happiness was indisputable. He was quite delighted. It
was the very circumstance he could have wished for. Now, it would be
really having Frank in their neighbourhood. What were nine miles to a
young man?—An hour’s ride. He would be always coming over. The
difference in that respect of Richmond and London was enough to make

serious obstacle. Were he ever able to get away, the day would be spent

Making my way along here with all despatch, I
had just crossed a ditch which I knew to be very near the Battery, and
had just scrambled up the mound beyond the ditch, when I saw the man
sitting before me. His back was towards me, and he had his arms folded,
and was nodding forward, heavy with sleep.

I thought he would be more glad if I came upon him with his breakfast,
in that unexpected manner, so I went forward softly and touched him on
the shoulder. He instantly jumped up, and it was not the same man, but
another man!

And yet this man was dressed in coarse grey, too, and had a great iron
on his leg, and was lame, and hoarse, and cold, and was everything that
the other man was; except that he had not the same face, and had a flat
broad-brimmed low-crowned felt hat on. All this I saw in a moment, for
I had only a moment to see it in: he swore an oath at me, made a hit at
me,—it was a round weak blow that missed me and almost knocked himself
down, for it made him stumble,—and then he ran into the mist, stumbling
twice as he went, and I lost him.

“It’s the young man!” I thought, feeling my heart shoot as I identified
him. I dare say I should have felt a pain in my liver, too, if I had
known where it was.

I was soon at the Battery after that, and there was the right
man,—hugging himself and limping to and fro, as if he had never all
night left off hugging and limping,—waiting for me. He was awfully
cold, to be sure. I half expected to see him drop down before my face
and die of deadly cold. His eyes looked so awfully hungry too, that
when I handed him the file and he laid it down on the grass, it
occurred to me he would have tried to eat it, if he had not seen my
bundle. He did not turn me upside down this time to get at what I had,
but left me right side upwards while I opened the bundle and emptied my
pockets.

“What’s in the bottle, boy?” said he.

“Brandy,” said I.

He was already handing mincemeat down his throat in the most curious
manner,—more like a man who was putting it away somewhere in a violent
hurry, than a man who was eating it,—but he left off to take some of
the liquor. He shivered all the while so violently, that it was quite
as much as he could do to keep the neck of the bottle between his
teeth, without biting it off.

“I think you have got the ague,” said I.

“I’m much of your opinion, boy,” said he.

“It’s bad about here,” I told him. “You’ve been lying out on the
meshes, and they’re dreadful aguish. Rheumatic too.”

“I’ll eat my breakfast afore they’re the death of me,” said he. “I’d do
that, if I was going to be strung up to that there gallows as there is
over there, directly afterwards. I’ll beat the shivers so far, I’ll bet
you.”

He was gobbling mincemeat, meatbone, bread, cheese, and pork pie, all
at once: staring distrustfully while he did so at the mist all round
us, and often stopping—even stopping his jaws—to listen.

The sergeant tossed off his glass again and seemed quite ready for
another glass. I noticed that Mr. Pumblechook in his hospitality
appeared to forget that he had made a present of the wine, but took the
bottle from Mrs. Joe and had all the credit of handing it about in a
gush of joviality. Even I got some. And he was so very free of the wine
that he even called for the other bottle, and handed that about with
the same liberality, when the first was gone.

As I watched them while they all stood clustering about the forge,
enjoying themselves so much, I thought what terrible good sauce for a
dinner my fugitive friend on the marshes was. They had not enjoyed
themselves a quarter so much, before the entertainment was brightened
with the excitement he furnished. And now, when they were all in lively
anticipation of “the two villains” being taken, and when the bellows
seemed to roar for the fugitives, the fire to flare for them, the smoke
to hurry away in pursuit of them, Joe to hammer and clink for them, and
all the murky shadows on the wall to shake at them in menace as the
blaze rose and sank, and the red-hot sparks dropped and died, the pale
afternoon outside almost seemed in my pitying young fancy to have
turned pale on their account, poor wretches.

At last, Joe’s job was done, and the ringing and roaring stopped. As
Joe got on his coat, he mustered courage to propose that some of us
should go down with the soldiers and see what came of the hunt. Mr.
Pumblechook and Mr. Hubble declined, on the plea of a pipe and ladies’
society; but Mr. Wopsle said he would go, if Joe would. Joe said he was
agreeable, and would take me, if Mrs. Joe approved. We never should
have got leave to go, I am sure, but for Mrs. Joe’s curiosity to know
all about it and how it ended. As it was, she merely stipulated, “If
you bring the boy back with his head blown to bits by a musket, don’t
look to me to put it together again.”

The sergeant took a polite leave of the ladies, and parted from Mr.
Pumblechook as from a comrade; though I doubt if he were quite as fully
sensible of that gentleman’s merits under arid conditions, as when
something moist was going. His men resumed their muskets and fell in.
Mr. Wopsle, Joe, and I, received strict charge to keep in the rear, and
to speak no word after we reached the marshes. When we were all out in
the raw air and were steadily moving towards our business, I
treasonably whispered to Joe, “I hope, Joe, we shan’t find them.” and
Joe whispered to me, “I’d give a shilling if they had cut and run,
Pip.”

We were joined by no stragglers from the village, for the weather was

There we were stopped a few minutes by a signal from the sergeant’s

I leaned over Joe, and, with the aid of my forefinger read him the

“I don’t spell it at all,” said Joe.

“It _can’t_ be supposed,” said Joe. “Tho’ I’m uncommon fond of reading,

“On-common. Give me,” said Joe, “a good book, or a good newspaper, and

“Why didn’t you ever go to school, Joe, when you were as little as me?”

“Well, Pip,” said Joe, taking up the poker, and settling himself to his

“Consequence, my mother and me we ran away from my father several

I didn’t see; but I didn’t say so.

“Well!” Joe pursued, “somebody must keep the pot a-biling, Pip, or the

I saw that, and said so.

“Consequence, my father didn’t make objections to my going to work; so

“I am not sure that I shouldn’t like to see her again, but I should

“You shall go soon,” said Miss Havisham, aloud. “Play the game out.”

Saving for the one weird smile at first, I should have felt almost sure

within and without, under the weight of a crushing blow.

I played the game to an end with Estella, and she beggared me. She
threw the cards down on the table when she had won them all, as if she
despised them for having been won of me.

“When shall I have you here again?” said Miss Havisham. “Let me think.”

I was beginning to remind her that to-day was Wednesday, when she
checked me with her former impatient movement of the fingers of her
right hand.

“There, there! I know nothing of days of the week; I know nothing of
weeks of the year. Come again after six days. You hear?”

“Yes, ma’am.”

“Estella, take him down. Let him have something to eat, and let him
roam and look about him while he eats. Go, Pip.”

I followed the candle down, as I had followed the candle up, and she
stood it in the place where we had found it. Until she opened the side
entrance, I had fancied, without thinking about it, that it must
necessarily be night-time. The rush of the daylight quite confounded
me, and made me feel as if I had been in the candlelight of the strange
room many hours.

“You are to wait here, you boy,” said Estella; and disappeared and
closed the door.

I took the opportunity of being alone in the courtyard to look at my
coarse hands and my common boots. My opinion of those accessories was
not favourable. They had never troubled me before, but they troubled me
now, as vulgar appendages. I determined to ask Joe why he had ever
taught me to call those picture-cards Jacks, which ought to be called
knaves. I wished Joe had been rather more genteelly brought up, and
then I should have been so too.

She came back, with some bread and meat and a little mug of beer. She
put the mug down on the stones of the yard, and gave me the bread and
meat without looking at me, as insolently as if I were a dog in
disgrace.

“Well, miss?” I answered, almost falling over her and checking myself.

She stood looking at me, and, of course, I stood looking at her.

“Am I pretty?”

“Yes; I think you are very pretty.”

“Am I insulting?”

“Not so much so as you were last time,” said I.

“Not so much so?”

“No.”

She fired when she asked the last question, and she slapped my face
with such force as she had, when I answered it.

“Now?” said she. “You little coarse monster, what do you think of me
now?”

“I shall not tell you.”

“Because you are going to tell upstairs. Is that it?”

“No,” said I, “that’s not it.”

“Why don’t you cry again, you little wretch?”

“Because I’ll never cry for you again,” said I. Which was, I suppose,
as false a declaration as ever was made; for I was inwardly crying for
her then, and I know what I know of the pain she cost me afterwards.

We went on our way upstairs after this episode; and, as we were going
up, we met a gentleman groping his way down.

“Whom have we here?” asked the gentleman, stopping and looking at me.

“A boy,” said Estella.

He was a burly man of an exceedingly dark complexion, with an
exceedingly large head, and a corresponding large hand. He took my chin
in his large hand and turned up my face to have a look at me by the
light of the candle. He was prematurely bald on the top of his head,
and had bushy black eyebrows that wouldn’t lie down but stood up
bristling. His eyes were set very deep in his head, and were
disagreeably sharp and suspicious. He had a large watch-chain, and
strong black dots where his beard and whiskers would have been if he
had let them. He was nothing to me, and I could have had no foresight
then, that he ever would be anything to me, but it happened that I had
this opportunity of observing him well.

“Boy of the neighbourhood? Hey?” said he.

“Yes, sir,” said I.

“How do _you_ come here?”

“Miss Havisham sent for me, sir,” I explained.

“Well! Behave yourself. I have a pretty large experience of boys, and
you’re a bad set of fellows. Now mind!” said he, biting the side of his
great forefinger as he frowned at me, “you behave yourself!”

With those words, he released me—which I was glad of, for his hand
smelt of scented soap—and went his way downstairs. I wondered whether
he could be a doctor; but no, I thought; he couldn’t be a doctor, or he
would have a quieter and more persuasive manner. There was not much
time to consider the subject, for we were soon in Miss Havisham’s room,
where she and everything else were just as I had left them. Estella
left me standing near the door, and I stood there until Miss Havisham
cast her eyes upon me from the dressing-table.

“So!” she said, without being startled or surprised: “the days have
worn away, have they?”

“Yes, ma’am. To-day is—”

“There, there, there!” with the impatient movement of her fingers. “I
don’t want to know. Are you ready to play?”

I was obliged to answer in some confusion, “I don’t think I am, ma’am.”

Then, he and my sister would pair off in such nonsensical speculations
about Miss Havisham, and about what she would do with me and for me,
that I used to want—quite painfully—to burst into spiteful tears, fly
at Pumblechook, and pummel him all over. In these dialogues, my sister
spoke to me as if she were morally wrenching one of my teeth out at
every reference; while Pumblechook himself, self-constituted my patron,
would sit supervising me with a depreciatory eye, like the architect of
my fortunes who thought himself engaged on a very unremunerative job.

In these discussions, Joe bore no part. But he was often talked at,
while they were in progress, by reason of Mrs. Joe’s perceiving that he
was not favourable to my being taken from the forge. I was fully old
enough now to be apprenticed to Joe; and when Joe sat with the poker on
his knees thoughtfully raking out the ashes between the lower bars, my
sister would so distinctly construe that innocent action into
opposition on his part, that she would dive at him, take the poker out
of his hands, shake him, and put it away. There was a most irritating
end to every one of these debates. All in a moment, with nothing to
lead up to it, my sister would stop herself in a yawn, and catching
sight of me as it were incidentally, would swoop upon me with, “Come!
there’s enough of _you_! _You_ get along to bed; _you_’ve given trouble
enough for one night, I hope!” As if I had besought them as a favour to
bother my life out.

We went on in this way for a long time, and it seemed likely that we
should continue to go on in this way for a long time, when one day Miss
Havisham stopped short as she and I were walking, she leaning on my
shoulder; and said with some displeasure,—

“You are growing tall, Pip!”

I thought it best to hint, through the medium of a meditative look,
that this might be occasioned by circumstances over which I had no
control.

She said no more at the time; but she presently stopped and looked at
me again; and presently again; and after that, looked frowning and
moody. On the next day of my attendance, when our usual exercise was
over, and I had landed her at her dressing-table, she stayed me with a
movement of her impatient fingers:—

“Tell me the name again of that blacksmith of yours.”

“Joe Gargery, ma’am.”

“Meaning the master you were to be apprenticed to?”

“Yes, Miss Havisham.”

“You had better be apprenticed at once. Would Gargery come here with
you, and bring your indentures, do you think?”

I signified that I had no doubt he would take it as an honour to be
asked.

“Then let him come.”

“At any particular time, Miss Havisham?”

“There, there! I know nothing about times. Let him come soon, and come
along with you.”

When I got home at night, and delivered this message for Joe, my sister
“went on the Rampage,” in a more alarming degree than at any previous
period. She asked me and Joe whether we supposed she was door-mats
under our feet, and how we dared to use her so, and what company we
graciously thought she _was_ fit for?

He lodged at a sluice-keeper’s out on the marshes,
and on working-days would come slouching from his hermitage, with his
hands in his pockets and his dinner loosely tied in a bundle round his
neck and dangling on his back. On Sundays he mostly lay all day on the
sluice-gates, or stood against ricks and barns. He always slouched,
locomotively, with his eyes on the ground; and, when accosted or
otherwise required to raise them, he looked up in a half-resentful,
half-puzzled way, as though the only thought he ever had was, that it
was rather an odd and injurious fact that he should never be thinking.

This morose journeyman had no liking for me. When I was very small and
timid, he gave me to understand that the Devil lived in a black corner
of the forge, and that he knew the fiend very well: also that it was
necessary to make up the fire, once in seven years, with a live boy,
and that I might consider myself fuel. When I became Joe’s ’prentice,
Orlick was perhaps confirmed in some suspicion that I should displace
him; howbeit, he liked me still less. Not that he ever said anything,
or did anything, openly importing hostility; I only noticed that he
always beat his sparks in my direction, and that whenever I sang Old
Clem, he came in out of time.

Dolge Orlick was at work and present, next day, when I reminded Joe of
my half-holiday. He said nothing at the moment, for he and Joe had just
got a piece of hot iron between them, and I was at the bellows; but by
and by he said, leaning on his hammer,—

“Now, master! Sure you’re not a-going to favour only one of us. If
Young Pip has a half-holiday, do as much for Old Orlick.” I suppose he
was about five-and-twenty, but he usually spoke of himself as an
ancient person.

“Why, what’ll you do with a half-holiday, if you get it?” said Joe.

“What’ll _I_ do with it! What’ll _he_ do with it? I’ll do as much with
it as _him_,” said Orlick.

“As to Pip, he’s going up town,” said Joe.

“Well then, as to Old Orlick, _he_’s a-going up town,” retorted that
worthy. “Two can go up town. Tain’t only one wot can go up town.

“Don’t lose your temper,” said Joe.

“Shall if I like,” growled Orlick. “Some and their uptowning! Now,
master! Come. No favouring in this shop. Be a man!”

The master refusing to entertain the subject until the journeyman was
in a better temper, Orlick plunged at the furnace, drew out a red-hot
bar, made at me with it as if he were going to run it through my body,
whisked it round my head, laid it on the anvil, hammered it out,—as if
