"That's my name—what's the problem?"

"Nothing," the voice replied, and the man kept coming.

I held my lamp out over the rail, and he stepped slowly into its light. It was a shaded lamp meant for reading, so the circle of light was very small; he was in it for just a moment before stepping out again. In that instant I saw a face that was unfamiliar to me, looking up with an incomprehensible expression of being touched and pleased to see me.

The wind had been so fierce that the lead was ripped off the roofs of tall city buildings. In the countryside, trees were uprooted, windmill sails were blown away, and reports from the coast spoke of shipwrecks and deaths. Heavy rain fell with the wind, and the day that ended as I sat down to read was the worst of all.

Since then the Temple has been changed, and it is no longer as isolated or as close to the river as it once was. We lived at the top of the last house, and that night the wind rushing up the river shook the house like cannon fire or a breaking sea. When the rain hit the windows, I looked up at them as they rattled and imagined I was inside a storm‑battered lighthouse. Occasionally smoke curled down the chimney as if it could not leave in such a night. When I opened the doors and looked down the staircase, the stair lamps were out. I covered my face with my hands and peered through the dark windows—opening them even a little was impossible in that wind and rain—and saw that the courtyard lamps were out, the lamps on the bridges and shore were flickering, and the coal fires on barges in the river were being blown out like red‑hot splashes in the rain.

I read with my watch on the table, planning to close my book at eleven o’clock. As I shut it, Saint Paul’s and the many church clocks in the city began to strike the hour. The wind made the sound sound strange, and I was listening, thinking about how the wind battered and tore at it, when I heard a footstep on the stairs.

I don’t know why I jumped, thinking of my dead sister’s footstep, but the sound faded quickly. I listened again and heard the footstep coming up, stumbling. Remembering that the stair lamps were out, I took my reading lamp and went to the top of the stairs. Whoever was below stopped when they saw my lamp, and everything was quiet.

"Is there someone down there?" I called, looking down.

"Yes," a voice answered from the darkness.

"Which floor do you want?"

"The top. Mr. Pip."

"That’s my name—what’s the matter?"

"Nothing," the voice replied, and the man kept coming up.

I held my lamp over the rail, and he stepped slowly into its light. My lamp was a small shaded one meant for reading, so the circle of light was narrow; he was in it for only a moment before stepping out again. In that brief instant I saw a face I didn’t recognize, looking up with a strange, pleased expression at seeing me.

When we judge an author's merit and assign him his place among our literary deities, we may view him through our own perspective and measure him by our own criteria. Yet, in assessing the power evident in his works, we must follow his own intentions, placing his creations beside his own ideal to see what is lacking. Our view of art differs from Mr. Poe's. He holds that art should be the production of Beauty, and perhaps we only disagree on the definition of that term. In evaluating his writings, however, we shall employ his own standard as our guide. The temple of the god of song is open on every side, and there is ample space within for all who bring offerings or seek an oracle.

In his stories, Mr. Poe chooses to display his talent chiefly in that shadowy zone that stretches from the farthest reaches of the plausible into the strange realms of superstition and unreality. He unites, in a striking fashion, two faculties rarely found together: the ability to sway the reader's mind with the intangible shadows of mystery, and a meticulous attention to detail that spares no pin or button. Both arise, in truth, from the dominant quality of his mind, which we have earlier termed analysis. It is this that sets the artist apart. His mind simultaneously looks ahead to the effect he wishes to produce. Having decided which emotions to evoke, he makes every subordinate element march toward that single centre. Even his mystery is mathematically precise to his own intellect. To him, X is a known quantity from the start. In any picture he paints he knows the chemical properties of each colour. No matter how vague his figures may appear, no matter how formless the shadows, to him the outline is as clear as a geometric diagram. For this reason Mr. Poe has no sympathy for Mysticism. The Mystic lives within mystery, is wrapped in it; it colours all his thoughts, tinges his vision, and even the most ordinary things acquire a rainbow fringe. Mr. Poe, by contrast, is a spectator _ab extra_. He analyses, he dissects, he watches

“with an eye serene,
The very pulse of the machine,”

for to him it is practically that—a mechanism of wheels, cogs, and piston‑rods, all working toward a definite end.

This analytical bent balances his poetic side, and by granting him the patience for minutiae, it lets him cast a marvelous reality into his most unreal fantasies. He paints a monomania with great vigor. He delights in dissecting one of those mental cancers and tracing every subtle branch of its roots. In conjuring images of horror he also achieves a strange success, often delivering, through a dim hint, a terrible doubt that lies at the heart of all terror. He leaves the completion of the picture to imagination, a task to which only she is truly suited.

“For much imaginary work was there;
Conceit deceitful, so compact, so kind,
That for Achilles’ image stood his spear
Grasped in an armed hand; himself behind
Was left unseen, save to the eye of mind.”

My principal ambition is to launch a periodical to be titled “The Stylus,” yet it would be of no use to me—once established—if it were not wholly free from a publisher’s control. In other words, I intend to create a journal that will be entirely my own in every respect. To achieve this, I must first secure a list of at least five hundred subscribers; I already have nearly two hundred. I plan, however, to travel South and West among my personal and literary acquaintances—old college mates and West Point friends—and see what can be done. To raise the necessary funds for the initial step, I intend to give a lecture at the Society Library on Thursday, the 3rd of February, and, to avoid any quarrel, my topic will not be literary at all. I have selected a broad subject: “The Universe.”

Having now presented you with the facts of the matter, I leave the remainder to the judgment of your own tact and generosity. With deepest gratitude,

Your ever‑faithful friend,
EDGAR A. POE.

Although these letters are brief and written on a whim, we think they sufficiently demonstrate the very qualities that are denied to Mr. Poe—humility, perseverance, belief in another’s friendship, and the capacity for warm and grateful companionship. He possessed these traits when he was sane, and they are the only aspects we have consistently observed in the five or six years we have known him personally. It is far easier to trust what we have seen and experienced than what we hear from others; consequently we remember him with admiration and respect. The portrayals of him made during his periods of mental instability seem, to us, like portraits painted in sickness of a man we only ever knew in health.

Yet there is another, more moving and far more compelling piece of evidence that genuine goodness existed in Edgar A. Poe. To reveal it we must lift the veil that solemnly covers grief and refinement in poverty; we believe this may be justified if it helps brighten the poet’s memory, even if it does not serve a more immediate purpose for those whose lives were broken by his death.

Our first notice of Mr. Poe’s relocation to this city came via a call from a lady who introduced herself as his mother‑in‑law. She was seeking employment for him and justified her request by mentioning his illness, her daughter’s chronic invalidity, and the circumstances that forced her to intervene. The lady’s countenance, made beautiful and saintly by an evident surrender of her life to hardship and tender sorrow, her gentle, mournful voice pleading the case, her long‑forgotten yet instinctively refined manners, and her appealing yet appreciative reference to her son’s talents and claims, at once revealed the presence of one of those earthly angels that women in distress can become.

It was a hard fate she was overseeing. Mr. Poe wrote with painstaking care, his style elevated far above popular taste, which made it difficult for him to earn a decent living.

After about four and a half hours the balloon was sufficiently inflated, so I fastened the carriage to it and loaded all my gear—making sure not to omit the condensing apparatus, a generous supply of water, and a large stock of pemmican, which packs a great deal of nourishment into a small volume. I also placed a pair of pigeons and a cat in the carriage. Dawn was nearly upon us, and I felt it was the proper moment to depart. I pretended to drop a lit cigar on the ground, and while stooping to retrieve it I secretly ignited the slow‑match whose tip, as I have mentioned, projected only a little beyond the lower rim of one of the smaller casks. The three duns observed nothing, and as soon as I leapt into the carriage I cut the single cord that tethered me to the earth, delighted to find that I rose swiftly, bearing with ease one hundred and seventy‑five pounds of lead ballast, and capable of taking even more.

 scarcely had I reached a height of fifty yards when a terrible, roaring hurricane of flame, smoke, sulphur, limbs, gravel, burning wood, and blazing metal surged after me in a most dreadful and tumultuous fashion. My heart sank, and I fell to the bottom of the carriage trembling with unmitigated terror. It became clear that I had greatly exceeded the limits of my experiment and that the worst of the shock was still to come. In an instant the blood rushed to my temples, and a concussion—one I shall never forget—burst through the night, seeming to tear the very firmament asunder. Later, when I could reflect, I saw that the ferocity of the explosion was due to my position directly above it, in the line of its greatest force. At that moment, however, I thought only of saving my life. The balloon first collapsed, then violently expanded, then spun round and round with dreadful speed, and finally, reeling like a drunkard, flung me with great force over the rim of the carriage. I was left hanging at a terrible height, head down and face outward, by a slender cord about three feet long that had slipped through a crack near the bottom of the wickerwork, and as I fell my left foot became providentially caught in it. No mind can form an adequate picture of the horror of my plight. I gasped convulsively for breath, a shudder like a fit of ague shaking every nerve and muscle, my eyes seemed to pop from their sockets, a horrible nausea overwhelmed me, and at last I fainted.

How long I remained in that state I cannot say; it must have been a considerable interval, for when I began to regain a sense of being, I found day breaking, the balloon soaring at a prodigious altitude over a boundless ocean, with not a hint of land to be seen anywhere within the vast horizon.

“Having taken this attitude toward the matter, I felt little further hesitation. Assuming that, during my ascent, I would encounter an atmosphere essentially like that at the earth’s surface, I imagined that, by means of M. Grimm’s clever device, I could easily condense enough of it for breathing. This would eliminate the principal obstacle to a lunar voyage. I had indeed spent money and considerable effort adapting the apparatus for this purpose, and I looked forward with confidence to its successful use, provided I could complete the journey within a reasonable time. This brings me back to the question of how fast the travel might be.

“It is true that balloons, in the early stages of their rise from the earth, are known to ascend at a comparatively moderate speed. The lifting power comes entirely from the great lightness of the gas in the balloon compared with the surrounding air; and at first glance it seems unlikely that, as the balloon climbs and enters layers of air whose density falls rapidly, the original speed would increase. Yet I was not aware of any recorded ascent in which the absolute rate of rise decreased; such a decline should have occurred, if only because of gas leakage from poorly constructed balloons varnished with ordinary varnish. It seemed, therefore, that the loss of gas merely offset whatever accelerating force might be present. I now thought that, if in my passage I found the medium I had imagined, and if it proved to be essentially what we call atmospheric air, the degree of rarefaction—no matter how extreme—would make little difference to my ascent. The gas in the balloon would itself become rarified in proportion, allowing enough escape to prevent explosion, yet it would remain lighter than any mixture of nitrogen and oxygen. Meanwhile, the pull of gravity would steadily lessen in proportion to the square of the distance, so with a rapidly increasing velocity I would eventually reach those remote zones where the earth’s attraction is outweighed by the moon’s. With these ideas, I saw no reason to burden myself with more provisions than would suffice for forty days.

“There was, however, another difficulty that caused me some unease. It has been noted that, in balloon ascents to considerable heights, besides the difficulty of breathing, great discomfort is felt in the head and body, often accompanied by nosebleeds and other alarming symptoms, which become increasingly troublesome as altitude increases.”

This process, repeated many times, eventually filled the chamber with an atmosphere suitable for breathing. Yet, in such a confined space the air would soon become foul and unsuitable for the lungs. It was then expelled through a small valve at the bottom of the car, the dense air sinking into the thinner atmosphere below. To avoid creating a complete vacuum at any instant, the purification was never done all at once; the valve was opened only a few seconds at a time, then shut again, until one or two strokes of the condenser’s pump had replaced the expelled air. For the experiment I placed the cat and its kittens in a small basket, hanging it outside the car by a button near the valve, through which I could feed them whenever necessary. I did this with some risk, and before sealing the chamber I reached beneath the car with one of the previously mentioned poles, to which a hook had been attached.

"When I had finally finished these preparations and filled the chamber as described, only ten minutes remained until nine o’clock. Throughout the whole period I suffered the most terrible distress from difficulty of breathing, and I bitterly repented the negligence—or rather the foolish obstinacy—with which I had postponed such an important matter. Yet, after at last completing it, I soon began to enjoy the benefits of my invention. Once more I breathed freely and easily—and why should I not? I was also pleasantly surprised to find that, to a great extent, the violent pains that had hitherto tormented me were relieved. A slight headache, together with a feeling of fullness about the wrists, ankles, and throat, was nearly all I had left to complain of. It seemed clear, then, that most of the discomfort accompanying the loss of atmospheric pressure had indeed subsided, as I had expected, and that much of the pain endured during the previous two hours must have been due entirely to deficient respiration.

"Twenty minutes before nine o’clock—that is, shortly before I sealed the chamber’s mouth—the mercury reached its limit, or fell, in the barometer, which, as I have noted, was of an extended design. It then indicated an altitude of 132,000 feet, or twenty‑five miles, and at that moment I could survey an area of the earth amounting to no less than three‑hundred‑and‑twentieth of its total surface. At nine o’clock I again lost sight of land to the east, but not before noticing that the balloon was rapidly drifting toward the north‑north‑west. The convex curve of the ocean beneath me was very evident, though my view was often broken by the masses of cloud that floated to and fro.

I found myself more persuaded by the second view. The icy rim to the north grew ever more distinct, though the cold was not exceedingly severe. Nothing noteworthy transpired, and I spent the day in reading, having taken care to provision myself with books.

"April 5th. Observed the curious spectacle of the sun's ascent while almost the whole visible face of the earth remained shrouded in darkness. In time the light spread over everything, and once more I discerned the line of ice to the north. It now stood very clear, of a darker shade than the ocean's waters. I was evidently drawing nearer, and with great speed. I fancied I could again make out a strip of land to the east, and another to the west, though I could not be certain. Weather moderate. No event of consequence occurred during the day. Retired early to bed.

"April 6th. Was astonished to find the ice rim at a very moderate distance, and an immense expanse of the same substance stretching to the horizon in the north. It was clear that, should the balloon maintain its present course, it would soon pass over the Frozen Ocean, and I now had little doubt of eventually seeing the Pole. Throughout the day I continued to approach the ice. Toward evening the limits of my horizon suddenly and markedly expanded, undoubtedly due to the earth's shape as an oblate spheroid, and my ascent above the flattened region near the Arctic Circle. When darkness finally overtook me, I went to bed in great anxiety, fearing that I might cross the object of such curiosity without the chance to observe it.

"April 7th. Rose early, and to my great delight at last beheld what could not be mistaken for anything but the northern Pole itself. It lay there, beyond doubt, directly beneath my feet; yet, alas, I had risen to such a height that nothing could be discerned with precision. In any case I unquestionably beheld the whole of the earth's major diameter; the entire northern hemisphere lay beneath me like an orthographic chart, and the great circle of the equator formed the boundary of my horizon. Your Excellencies may, however, readily imagine that the confined regions still unexplored within the Arctic Circle, though situated directly beneath me and thus seen without foreshortening, remained, in themselves, comparatively small and at too great a distance from the point of view to permit any very accurate examination."

This, indeed, is the case. I possess a great—indeed a very great—amount of information which I would take the utmost pleasure in conveying. I have much to report about the planet’s climate; its marvelous swings between heat and cold, the unrelenting, scorching sunshine that lasts a fortnight and then gives way to a chill far beyond polar frost; the continual movement of moisture, distilled as if in a vacuum, from the point directly under the sun to the point farthest from it; the shifting streams of water; the inhabitants themselves; their manners, customs, and political structures; their odd physical make‑up; their ugliness; their lack of ears—those useless appendages in an atmosphere so peculiarly altered; their resulting ignorance of speech’s use and properties; their replacement for speech in a singular mode of inter‑communication; the incomprehensible link between each individual on the moon and a particular individual on Earth—a connection analogous to, and dependent upon, that of the planet’s orbs and its satellites, by which the lives and destinies of one’s inhabitants are intertwined with those of the other; and above all, if it pleases your Excellencies—above all, those dark and hideous mysteries that lie in the moon’s outer regions—areas that, because of the almost miraculous synchrony of the satellite’s rotation on its axis with its sidereal revolution around Earth, have never been turned toward, and, by God’s mercy, never shall be turned toward, the scrutiny of man’s telescopes. All this, and far more—much more—I would gladly detail. Yet, to be concise, I must ask for my reward. I yearn to return to my family and my home; and as the price for any further communication on my part—considering the light I can shed on many crucial branches of physical and metaphysical science—I must, through the influence of your honorable body, request a pardon for the crime I committed in the death of the creditors when I left Rotterdam. This, then, is the purpose of the present paper. Its bearer, a moon inhabitant whom I have persuaded and properly instructed to act as my messenger to Earth, will await your Excellencies’ pleasure and return to me with the pardon, if it can in any way be obtained.

“I have the honor to be, etc., your Excellencies’ very humble servant,

“HANS PFAALL.”

When Professor Rub‑a‑dub finished reading this most extraordinary document, it is said he dropped his pipe in astonishment, and Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk, having removed his spectacles, wiped them and slipped them into his pocket, so completely forgot himself and his dignity that he turned three times on his heel in sheer amazement and admiration. There was no doubt about the matter—the pardon must be secured. Thus, with a solemn oath, Professor Rub‑a‑dub swore, and the illustrious Von Underduk, taking his brother in science by the arm, said nothing further and set off for home to contemplate the measures to be taken.

When I reached the hut I knocked, as I always did, and, receiving no answer, I went looking for the hidden key, unlocked the door and entered. A bright fire burned in the hearth, a pleasant and not at all unwelcome sight. I shed my overcoat, settled into an arm‑chair beside the crackling logs, and waited patiently for my hosts to appear.

Soon after night fell they came, greeting me with great warmth. Jupiter, smiling from ear to ear, bustled about preparing some marsh‑hens for supper. Legrand was in one of his fits—how else shall I call them?—of enthusiasm. He had discovered an unknown bivalve, a new genus, and, more importantly, he and Jupiter had captured a scarab he believed to be entirely new, for which he wanted my opinion the next day.

"Why not tonight?" I asked, rubbing my hands over the fire and cursing the whole tribe of scarabaeids.
"Ah, if only I had known you were coming!" Legrand replied. "It has been ages since I saw you, and how could I have guessed you would visit on this very night? On my way home I met Lieutenant G—— from the fort and, foolishly, I lent him the bug; so you won’t be able to see it until morning. Stay here tonight, and I’ll have Jupiter fetch it at sunrise. It’s the loveliest thing in creation!"
"What?—sunrise?"
"Nonsense! No!—the bug. It’s a brilliant gold, about the size of a large hickory‑nut, with two jet‑black spots near one end of its back and another, a little longer, at the opposite end. The antennae are—"
"Dey ain’t no tin in him, Massa Will, I keep a tellin’ on you," interrupted Jupiter. "De bug is a good‑lookin’ bug, solid, every bit of him, inside and out, sep him wing—never felt half so heavy a bug in my life."
"Well, suppose it is, Jup," Legrand answered, a touch more earnestly than the matter required. "Is that any reason for you letting the birds burn? The colour—" he turned to me, "—is almost enough to justify Jupiter’s idea. You have never seen a more brilliant metallic luster than the scales emit—but you can’t judge that until tomorrow. In the meantime I can give you an idea of its shape." He sat at a small table that held a pen and ink but no paper. He searched a drawer, found none, and then said, "Never mind, this will do;" pulling from his waistcoat pocket a scrap of what seemed a very dirty foolscap, he sketched a rough picture with the pen. While he worked I stayed by the fire, still a little cold. When he finished, he handed the drawing to me without standing. As I took it, a loud growl sounded, followed by scratching at the door. Jupiter opened it, and a large Newfoundland belonging to Legrand burst in, leapt onto my shoulders, and showered me with affection, for I had shown him much kindness on earlier visits.

I feared that the relentless weight of misfortune might finally have shaken my friend's mind. Without a second thought, I readied myself to go with the negro.

When we reached the dock, I saw a scythe and three spades, all apparently brand‑new, lying at the bottom of the boat we were to board.

"What’s the purpose of all this, Jup?" I asked.

"Him syfe, massa, and spade," he answered.

"That’s right, but why are they here?"

"Him de syfe and de spade what Massa Will sis pon my buying for him in de town, and de debbil’s own lot of money I had to gib for ’em."

"But what on earth is your ‘Massa Will’ going to do with a scythe and spades?"

"Dat’s more dan _I_ know, and debbil take me if I don’t b’lieve ’tis more dan he know, too. But it’s all cum ob do bug."

Realizing that Jupiter could not give me a satisfactory answer—his mind seemed wholly occupied by "de bug"—I stepped into the boat and set out. A strong, steady breeze carried us quickly to a small cove north of Fort Moultrie, and after a two‑mile walk we reached the hut. It was about three o’clock in the afternoon when we arrived. Legrand was waiting for us, his anticipation evident. He seized my hand with a nervous eagerness that both startled me and confirmed my growing suspicions. His face was pallid to the point of ghastliness, and his deep‑set eyes shone with an uncanny gleam. After asking after his health, I, at a loss for better words, inquired whether he had finally obtained the _scarabæus_ from Lieutenant G——.

"Oh, yes," he replied, flushing fiercely, "I got it from him the next morning. Nothing will make me part with that _scarabæus_. Do you know that Jupiter is quite right about it?"

"In what way?" I asked, a foreboding heaviness settling in my heart.

"In thinking it to be a bug of _real gold_." He said this with solemn gravity, and I was struck beyond words.

"This bug will make my fortune," he continued, a triumphant smile spreading, "restore me to my family’s estate. Is it any wonder I cherish it? Since Fortune has deemed me worthy of it, I need only use it wisely and I shall reach the gold of which it is a sign. Jupiter; bring me that _scarabæus_!"

"What! the bug, massa? I’d not go after that trouble—you must get it for yourself." This contemplation hinted at some significance—some relevance—in the death‑head. I also noted the shape of the parchment. Though one corner had been torn away by accident, it was evident that the original sheet was oblong. It was precisely the sort of slip that might be chosen for a memorandum—a record meant to be long remembered and carefully kept.

"But," I interjected, "you say the skull was not on the parchment when you made the beetle drawing. How then can you link the boat and the skull—since, as you admit, the skull must have been added (God only knows how or by whom) after you had sketched the scarab?"

"Ah, that is where the whole mystery turns; yet the secret, at this point, was relatively easy for me to solve. My reasoning was straightforward and led to a single conclusion. I thought, for instance: when I drew the scarab, no skull was visible on the parchment. After I finished the drawing I handed it to you and watched you closely until you returned it. You, therefore, did not create the skull, and no one else was present to do so. So it was not the work of a human hand. Yet it was done.

"At this stage of my reflections I tried to recall, and I did recall with perfect clarity, every incident that occurred around that time. The weather was chilly (a rare and fortunate circumstance!), and a fire burned brightly in the hearth. I was warm from exertion and sat near the table. You, however, had placed a chair close to the chimney. As I handed the parchment to you and you were examining it, Wolf, the Newfoundland, entered and leapt onto your shoulders. With your left hand you patted him and kept him at bay, while your right hand, still holding the parchment, allowed it to slip lazily between your knees, close to the fire. My first attempt was to separate the sentence according to the natural division intended by the cryptographer.

"You mean, to punctuate it?"

"Something of that sort."

"But how could one accomplish that?"

"I thought that the author had deliberately run his words together without any breaks to make the puzzle harder. Yet a man who is not overly sharp, while trying to achieve that aim, would almost certainly overdo it. When, during his writing, he reached a point where the subject naturally called for a pause or a period, he would be very likely to press his characters together more tightly than usual. If you examine the manuscript now, you will readily notice five instances of such unusual crowding. Using this clue, I divided the passage as follows: ‘A good glass in the Bishop’s hostel in the Devil’s seat—forty‑one degrees and thirteen minutes—northeast and by north—main branch seventh limb east side—shoot from the left eye of the death‑head—a bee‑line from the tree through the shot fifty feet out.’"

"Even with that division," I said, "I remain in the dark."

"It left me in the dark as well," Legrand replied, "for several days; during that time I made careful inquiries around Sullivan’s Island for any building called the ‘Bishop’s Hotel,’ having, of course, dropped the archaic term ‘hostel.’ Finding no information, I was about to broaden my search and adopt a more systematic approach when, one morning, it suddenly occurred to me that this ‘Bishop’s Hostel’ might refer to an old family named Bessop, who for ages had owned an ancient manor about four miles north of the island. I therefore went to the plantation and resumed my questioning among the older negroes there. At last one of the eldest women said she had heard of a place called Bessop’s Castle and thought she could lead me to it, though it was neither a castle nor a tavern but a high rock.

"I offered her a generous payment for her trouble, and after some hesitation she agreed to accompany me. We located it without much difficulty; after she left, I examined the spot. The ‘castle’ was an irregular grouping of cliffs and rocks—one of them striking for its height and its strangely artificial appearance. I climbed to its summit and then felt quite at a loss as to what to do next.

"While I was pondering, my eyes fell on a narrow ledge on the eastern face of the rock, perhaps a yard below the top where I stood. The ledge jutted out about eighteen inches and was no wider than a foot, while a niche in the cliff just above gave it a crude likeness to one of the hollow‑backed chairs used by our ancestors. I had no doubt that this was the ‘devil’s seat’ mentioned in the manuscript."

I beg your forgiveness; I had overlooked that Shakespeare will not thrive for another fifteen hundred and fifty years. Yet does not the sight of Epidaphne give me cause to call it grotesque?

“It is strongly fortified; in this it owes as much to nature as to art.”
Indeed.

“There are an enormous number of lofty palaces.”
There are.

“And the many temples, rich and splendid, could be set alongside the most celebrated of antiquity.”
All this I must concede. Still, there are countless mud‑huts and wretched shacks. Filth seems to cling to every kennel, and if it were not for the overpowering fumes of idolatrous incense, I am certain we would be assaulted by an intolerable stench. Have you ever seen streets so oppressively narrow, or houses so astonishingly tall? The shadows they cast are dreadful! It is fortunate that the swinging lamps in those endless colonnades stay lit all day; otherwise we would be plunged into an Egyptian darkness in its desolation.

“It is certainly a strange place! What is the purpose of that lone building? Look! It rises above all the rest and stands to the east of what I presume is the royal palace!”
That is the new Temple of the Sun, worshipped in Syria under the name Elah Gabalah. A future notorious Roman emperor will adopt this cult in Rome and take the name Heliogabalus. I suspect you would like to glimpse the deity of the temple. You need not look to the heavens; his Sunship is not there—at least not the Sunship venerated by the Syrians. The god resides inside that building, represented by a massive stone pillar that terminates in a cone or pyramid, symbolizing Fire.

“Hark—look!—who are those ridiculous figures, half‑naked, faces painted, shouting and gesturing at the crowd?”
A few are mountebanks. Others belong more specifically to the class of philosophers. The greatest number, however—those who especially pester the populace with clubs—are the chief courtiers of the palace, performing, as duty demands, a kind of comic display for the king.

“But what is this? By the heavens! The town teems with wild beasts! What a terrible spectacle!—how dangerous a curiosity!”
Terrible, perhaps, but not at all dangerous. Each animal, if you take the trouble to watch, follows quietly in the wake of its master. Some are indeed led by a rope around the neck, but those are mainly the smaller or timider species. The lion, tiger, and leopard are completely unrestrained. They have been trained without difficulty for their present role and attend their owners as personal attendants. It is true that on occasion Nature asserts her untamed dominion; yet the devouring of a soldier or the throttling of a sacred bull is a fleeting incident, mentioned only in passing in Epidaphne.

“But what extraordinary uproar do I hear? Surely this is a clamor even for Antioch! It suggests a commotion of unusual interest.”

THE MURDERS IN THE RUE MORGUE

"What song the Syrens sang, or what name Achilles took when he concealed himself among women, though puzzling questions, are not beyond all conjecture."
—Sir Thomas Browne.

The mental qualities described as analytical are, in themselves, scarcely amenable to analysis. We perceive them only through their effects. We know, among other things, that when a mind is overly possessed by them they become a source of the keenest pleasure. Just as a strong man revels in his physical power, delighting in exercises that call his muscles to work, so the analyst exults in the moral activity of untangling. He finds enjoyment even in the most trivial tasks that allow his talent to be exercised. He is attracted to riddles, puzzles, hieroglyphs; in each solution he displays a degree of acumen that seems, to ordinary perception, almost supernatural. His conclusions, produced by the very soul and essence of method, in truth possess the whole character of intuition.

The power of re‑solution is perhaps greatly strengthened by mathematical study, especially by that highest branch which, unjustly and merely because of its backward‑looking operations, has been styled, as if par excellence, analysis. Yet calculation is not in itself analysis. A chess‑player, for example, performs one without effort the other. Hence the game of chess, in its influence on mental character, is widely misunderstood. I am not now composing a treatise, but merely prefacing a somewhat singular narrative with observations drawn at random; I will therefore take the opportunity to assert that the higher faculties of reflective intellect are more decisively and more usefully exercised by the modest game of draughts than by all the elaborate frivolity of chess. In the latter, where the pieces possess different and bizarre motions, with various and shifting values, what is merely complex is often mistaken (a not uncommon error) for what is profound. Attention is called powerfully into play. If it flags even for an instant, an oversight is made, leading to injury or defeat. The possible moves are not only numerous but intricate, multiplying the chances of such oversights; and in nine cases out of ten it is the more concentrative rather than the more acute player who prevails. In draughts, on the contrary, where the moves are unique and vary little, the probability of inadvertence is reduced, and with attention comparatively idle, any advantage gained by either side is due to superior acumen. To be less abstract, imagine a game of draughts reduced to four kings, where, of course, no oversight can be expected. It is evident that here victory, with the players otherwise equal, can be decided only by some recherché maneuver, the result of a strong exertion of intellect. Deprived of ordinary resources, the analyst throws himself into the spirit of his opponent, identifies with it, and often at a glance perceives the sole methods—sometimes absurdly simple—by which he may lure the adversary into error or haste.

The mental traits we call analytical are, in themselves, hardly open to analysis. We notice them only by their effects. We know, among other things, that when they are overly strong they become a source of the liveliest enjoyment for their owner. Just as a strong man revels in his physical ability, delighting in exercises that put his muscles to work, so the analyst delights in the moral activity that untangles. He takes pleasure even in the most trivial tasks that let his talent play out. He loves riddles, puzzles, hieroglyphs; in solving each he shows a level of insight that seems almost supernatural to ordinary minds. His results, produced by the very soul and essence of method, truly have the air of intuition.

The power of resolution is probably greatly sharpened by mathematical study, especially by that highest branch, which has been unfairly labeled "analysis" simply because of its backward‑looking operations. Yet calculating is not the same as analyzing. A chess player, for example, does one without effort while doing the other. This means that the impact of chess on mental character is widely misunderstood. I am not writing a treatise now, only prefacing a somewhat unusual narrative with random observations; so I will take this chance to claim that the higher powers of reflective intellect are more clearly and usefully exercised by the modest game of draughts than by all the elaborate frivolity of chess. In chess, where the pieces move in different and bizarre ways and have varying values, complexity is often mistaken (a common error) for depth. Attention is called into strong play. If it lapses even for a moment, an oversight can cause injury or defeat. Because the possible moves are not only many but also intricate, the chance of such oversights multiplies; and in nine out of ten cases it is the more concentrated rather than the sharper player who wins. In draughts, on the contrary, where the moves are unique and vary little, the probability of mistakes is reduced, and with attention largely idle, any advantage comes from superior insight.

To be less abstract, imagine a game of draughts reduced to four kings, where, of course, no oversight is expected. It is clear that victory (with the players otherwise equal) can be decided only by some recherché move, the result of a strong mental effort. Deprived of ordinary resources, the analyst throws himself into his opponent’s mindset, identifies with it, and often sees at a glance the only methods—sometimes absurdly simple—by which he can lure the opponent into error or force a miscalculation.

“To this dreadful mystery there is, as yet, we think, no slightest clue.”

The next day's newspaper added these particulars.

“The Tragedy in the Rue Morgue.—Many persons have been examined in connection with this most extraordinary and terrifying affair” [The word ‘affaire’ has not yet, in France, that lightness of meaning which it carries with us], “but nothing at all has emerged to illuminate it. Below we give all the material testimony obtained.

“Pauline Dubourg, laundress, states that she has known both the deceased for three years, having laundered for them during that time. The old lady and her daughter seemed on good terms—very affectionate toward each other. They were excellent pay. She could not speak about their mode or means of living. She believed Madame L. earned a living by telling fortunes. She was reputed to have money saved. She never met any persons in the house when she called for the clothes or took them home. She was sure they had no servant employed. There appeared to be no furniture in any part of the building except on the fourth story.

“Pierre Moreau, tobacconist, states that he has been in the habit of selling small quantities of tobacco and snuff to Madame L. Espanaye for nearly four years. He was born in the neighbourhood and has always lived there. The deceased and her daughter had occupied the house in which the corpses were found for more than six years. It had formerly been occupied by a jeweller, who under‑let the upper rooms to various persons. The house belonged to Madame L. She became dissatisfied with the abuse of the premises by her tenant, and moved in herself, refusing to let any portion. The old lady was childish. The witness had seen the daughter five or six times during the six years. The two lived an exceedingly retired life—were reputed to have money. He had heard it said among the neighbours that Madame L. told fortunes—did not believe it. He had never seen any person enter the door except the old lady and her daughter, a porter once or twice, and a physician some eight or ten times.

“Many other persons, neighbours, gave evidence to the same effect. No one was spoken of as frequenting the house. It was not known whether there were any living connections of Madame L. and her daughter. The shutters of the front windows were seldom opened. Those in the rear were always closed, except for the large back room on the fourth story. The house was a good house—not very old.

“Isidore Musèt, gendarme, states that he was called to the house about three o’clock in the morning, and found some twenty or thirty persons at the gateway, endeavouring to gain admittance. He forced it open, at length, with a bayonet—not with a crowbar. He had but little difficulty in getting it open, on account of its being a double or folding gate, and bolted neither at bottom nor top. The shrieks continued until the gate was forced—and then suddenly ceased. They seemed to be screams of some person (or persons) in great agony—were loud and drawn out, not short and quick. The witness led the way up stairs. Upon reaching the first landing, he heard two voices in loud and angry contention—the one a gruff voice, the other much shriller—a very strange voice.”

text:
I could only concur with all of Paris in deeming them an unsolvable enigma. I saw no way to track down the murderer.

"We must not judge the means by this superficial scrutiny," Dupin said. "The Paris police, praised for their cleverness, are shrewd, but no more. Their investigations lack a consistent method beyond the impulse of the moment. They parade a multitude of measures, yet often these are so poorly suited to the task that they remind us of Monsieur Jourdain's request for his robe-de-chambre—pour mieux entendre la musique. Their results are sometimes surprising, but mostly stem from plain diligence and activity. When those qualities fail, their plans collapse. Take Vidocq, for instance; he was a keen guesser and a tenacious man. Yet, without cultivated reasoning, he constantly erred through the sheer intensity of his inquiries. He strained his sight by holding the object too near. He might discern one or two points with unusual clarity, but in doing so he inevitably lost the overall picture. Thus one can be too profound. Truth does not always lie in a well. In fact, regarding the more significant knowledge, I think it is invariably superficial. The depth resides in the valleys where we search, not on the mountain‑tops where it is found. The kinds of mistakes described are well illustrated by the observation of celestial bodies. To glance at a star sideways—viewing it with the outer parts of the retina, which are more prone to faint light impressions than the inner—gives a distinct view, the best appreciation of its brilliance—a brilliance that dims precisely as we stare at it directly. More rays strike the eye in the latter case, but the former offers a finer capacity for understanding. Excessive profundity confounds and weakens thought; one can even make Venus disappear from the heavens by looking too long, too intensely, or too directly.

"As for these murders, let us conduct some examinations ourselves before forming an opinion about them. An inquiry will give us amusement," [I thought the word odd in this context, but said nothing] "and, besides, Le Bon once rendered me a service for which I am not ungrateful. We will go and see the premises with our own eyes. I know G——, the Prefect of Police, and will have no trouble obtaining the needed permission."

The permission was secured, and we promptly set out for Rue Morgue. This is one of those wretched streets that lie between Rue Richelieu and Rue St. Roch. We arrived late in the afternoon, as this quarter lay far from where we lived. The house was easy to locate; many people were still standing on the opposite side of the street, staring at the closed shutters with idle curiosity.

The odor had never once faded. No link in the chain was defective. I had followed the secret to its final outcome—and that outcome was the nail. It looked, in every way, like its counterpart in the opposite window; yet that fact was utterly meaningless (no matter how convincing it might appear) when weighed against the fact that here, at this spot, the thread ended. “There must be something amiss with the nail,” I said. I touched it, and the head, together with about a quarter‑inch of the shank, snapped off in my hand. The remaining shank lay in the gimlet‑hole where it had broken. The break was old (its edges were encrusted with rust) and seemed to have been caused by a hammer blow, which had partially driven the nail’s head into the top of the lower sash. I carefully put that head back into the dent from which I had taken it, and the nail looked whole again—the crack was invisible. Pressing the spring, I lifted the sash a few inches; the head rose with it, staying firmly in its place. I shut the window, and the nail appeared perfectly whole once more.

“The puzzle, up to this point, was now solved. The murderer had fled through the window that faced the bed. Whether by accident or deliberately, the window had been left closed as he left, and the spring had caught it; the police had taken this spring for the nail, deeming further investigation unnecessary.

“The next issue is how he descended. I had already walked with you around the building and noted that about five and a half feet from the window in question runs a lightning rod. From that rod it would have been impossible for anyone to reach the window, let alone enter it. I did notice, however, that the fourth‑story shutters were of a special type known to Parisian carpenters as ‘ferrades’—rare today but common on very old houses in Lyons and Bordeaux. They resemble an ordinary door (a single panel, not folding), but the lower half is latticed or worked into an open trellis, giving an excellent handhold. In this case the shutters were a full three and a half feet wide. Viewed from the rear of the house, both were about half open, standing at right angles to the wall. The police, like me, probably examined the back of the building; yet, when they looked at these ferrades along their width (as they must have), they either failed to notice the great breadth itself or ignored it. Having convinced themselves that no exit could be made in that area, they naturally gave it only a cursory glance.

We mean you no harm whatsoever. I give you my word as a gentleman and as a Frenchman that we intend no injury. I am fully aware that you are innocent of the crimes in the Rue Morgue, though it would be false to say you have no connection to them at all. As I have already explained, I possess information about this case—information you could never have imagined. Here is the situation: you have done nothing you could have avoided, nothing that makes you culpable. You were not even guilty of theft, even though you could have stolen with impunity. You have nothing to hide, no reason for concealment. Yet honor obliges you to disclose everything you know. An innocent man is now locked up, accused of a crime for which you can identify the true perpetrator.

The sailor regained much of his composure as Dupin spoke, but his earlier boldness had vanished.

"So help me God!" he said after a short pause, "I will tell you everything I know about this matter;—but I do not expect you to believe half of what I say—I would be a fool to think otherwise. Still, I am innocent, and I will clear my name even if it costs me my life."

In essence, he recounted the following. He had recently sailed to the Indian Archipelago. A party of which he was a member landed in Borneo and ventured inland for pleasure. He and a companion captured an orang‑outang. When the companion died, the animal became his sole possession. After great difficulty, caused by the animal’s fierce resistance during the return voyage, he finally managed to lodge it safely at his Paris home, where, to avoid attracting the unpleasant curiosity of his neighbours, he kept it hidden until it recovered from a foot wound caused by a splinter on board ship. His ultimate plan was to sell it.

Returning home from a night of sailors’ revelry—actually the morning of the murder—he found the beast in his own bedroom, having escaped from an adjoining closet where it had been thought securely confined. Razor in hand and fully lathered, it stood before a mirror, apparently attempting to shave, a habit it had observed from its master through the closet’s key‑hole. Horrified by the sight of such a dangerous weapon in the grasp of a ferocious animal that seemed capable of using it, the man was momentarily at a loss. He was accustomed to calming the creature, even in its fiercest moods, with a whip, and he now resorted to that. At the sight of the whip, the orang‑outang sprang out of the room, down the stairs, and through an unfortunately open window onto the street.

The Frenchman chased after it in despair; the ape, still holding the razor, occasionally turned back to look at its pursuer and gestured, until the man nearly caught up with it.

After great difficulty—caused by the animal’s fierce resistance during the return trip—he finally managed to bring it safely to his home in Paris, where, to avoid attracting unwanted attention from his neighbors, he kept it hidden until it recovered from a foot wound caused by a splinter on the ship. His ultimate plan was to sell it.

Returning home from a night of sailors’ revelry—actually the morning of the murder—he found the beast in his own bedroom, having broken out of an adjoining closet where it had been thought securely confined. Razor in hand and fully lathered, it stood before a mirror, apparently trying to shave, something it had likely watched its master do through the closet’s keyhole. Terrified by the sight of such a dangerous weapon in the paws of a ferocious animal that seemed capable of using it, the man was momentarily at a loss for what to do. He was used to calming the creature, even in its fiercest moods, with a whip, and he resorted to that now. As soon as he saw it, the orang‑utan leapt through the bedroom door, down the stairs, and out a window that was unfortunately open, onto the street.

The Frenchman chased after it in desperation; the ape, still holding the razor, occasionally stopped to look back and gesture at its pursuer, until the man was almost upon it.

“We mean you no harm at all. I promise you, as a gentleman and as a Frenchman, that we do not intend to hurt you. I know you are innocent of the murders in the Rue Morgue, but you are still involved in some way. As I have already explained, I have information about this case that you could never have imagined. Here is the situation: you have done nothing you could have avoided, nothing that makes you guilty. You were not even a thief, even though you could have stolen without being caught. You have nothing to hide and no reason to hide anything. Yet, honor requires you to tell us everything you know. An innocent man is now in prison, accused of a crime that you can point out the real culprit for.”

The sailor had mostly regained his composure while Dupin spoke, but his earlier confidence had vanished.

“So help me God!” he said after a short pause. “I will tell you everything I know about this case; but I do not expect you to believe half of what I say—I would be a fool to think otherwise. Still, I am innocent, and I will keep my word even if I die for it.”

In the proclamation announcing the reward, a complete pardon was offered to any accomplice who would turn evidence against his partner; and wherever it was posted, a private notice from a citizens' committee was added, promising ten thousand francs in addition to the sum offered by the Prefecture. Thus the total bounty reached at least thirty thousand francs, an extraordinary amount when one considers the modest circumstances of the girl and the frequent occurrence, in large cities, of crimes like the one described.

No one now doubted that the mystery of this murder would soon be solved. Yet, although a few arrests were made that seemed to promise clarification, nothing was uncovered that could incriminate the suspected parties, and they were released immediately. Strangely enough, three weeks passed after the body was found without any light being shed on the case before even a rumor of the events that had so stirred public opinion reached Dupin and me. Engrossed in investigations that occupied all our attention, nearly a month had gone by since either of us had left the house, received a visitor, or even glanced at the leading political articles in the daily papers. The first notice of the murder came to us from G—— in person. He came early on the afternoon of July 13, 18—, and stayed until late at night. He was irritated by his continual failure to uncover the murderers. His reputation—he said with a distinctly Parisian flair—was at stake, even his honor. The public’s gaze was upon him, and there was truly no sacrifice he would not make to resolve the mystery. He concluded a somewhat humorous speech with a compliment on what he liked to call Dupin’s tact, and presented him with a direct, and certainly generous, proposal, the exact nature of which I do not feel at liberty to disclose, as it bears no relevance to the proper subject of my narrative.

My friend brushed off the compliment as best he could, but he accepted the proposal at once, even though its benefits were entirely provisional. With that matter settled, the Prefect immediately launched into an explanation of his own views, interspersing them with lengthy remarks on the evidence—evidence we had not yet received. He spoke at length, undeniably learned, while I ventured occasional suggestions as the night wore on drowsily. Dupin, seated calmly in his usual arm‑chair, embodied respectful attention. He wore spectacles throughout the interview, and a brief, sharp glance beneath their green lenses was enough to convince me that he slept no less soundly, for he remained silently attentive during the seven or eight heavy‑footed hours that preceded the Prefect’s departure.

The next morning I obtained at the Prefecture a complete report of all the evidence gathered, and at the various newspaper offices a copy of every paper that, from the first to the last, had published any decisive information concerning this tragic affair.

Nobody went over. Nothing was said or heard about the affair in the Rue Pavée St. Andrée that reached even the residents of the same building. M. St. Eustache, the lover and intended husband of Marie, who was lodging in her mother’s house, testifies that he did not learn of the discovery of his intended’s body until the next morning, when M. Beauvais entered his room and informed him. For a piece of news such as this, it is striking that he received it very calmly.

In this manner the journal tried to give the impression that Marie’s relatives were indifferent, a view at odds with the idea that they believed the corpse to be hers. Its insinuations suggest that Marie, with the collusion of her friends, had left the city for reasons involving a charge against her chastity; and that these friends, upon finding a body in the Seine that somewhat resembled the girl’s, seized the chance to convince the public of her death. Yet L’Etoile was again premature. It was clearly shown that no such indifference existed; that the old lady was extremely frail and so agitated that she could not attend to any duty; that St. Eustache, far from taking the news calmly, was overwhelmed with grief and behaved so frantically that M. Beauvais had to persuade a friend and relative to look after him and keep him from attending the examination at the disinterment. Moreover, although L’Etoile claimed that the corpse was re‑interred at public expense, that a generous offer of private sculpture had been outright refused by the family, and that no family member attended the ceremony—claims the paper used to reinforce its intended impression—each of these points was convincingly disproved. In a later issue the paper attempted to cast suspicion on Beauvais himself. The editor wrote:

“Now, then, a change comes over the matter. We are told that on one occasion, while a Madame B—— was at Madame Rogêt’s house, M. Beauvais, who was about to leave, told her that a gendarme was expected there, and she, Madame B., must not speak to the gendarme until he returned, but let the matter be for him.... In the present state of affairs, M. Beauvais appears to have the whole matter locked up in his head. No step can be taken without M. Beauvais, for, whichever way you go, you run into him.... For some reason, he decided that nobody should have anything to do with the proceedings but himself, and he has pushed the male relatives aside, according to their accounts, in a very singular fashion. He seems to have been strongly opposed to letting the relatives see the body.”

A fact was then offered to lend some color to the suspicion directed at Beauvais. A visitor to his office, a few days before the girl’s disappearance and during the occupant’s absence, had seen a rose placed in the key‑hole of the door and the name “Marie” written on a slate that hung nearby.

text:
To me, this article seems to amount to little more than the enthusiasm of its writer. We must remember that, in general, newspapers aim more at creating a sensation—to make a point—than at advancing truth. The latter is only pursued when it coincides with the former. Print that merely aligns with common opinion (no matter how well‑founded that opinion may be) gains no favor with the crowd. The masses consider only the one who offers _sharp contradictions_ of the prevailing view to be profound. In reasoning, as in literature, the epigram is the most instantly and universally admired. In both fields it ranks at the lowest level of merit.

"What I intend to say is that it is the mixture of epigram and melodrama surrounding the notion that Marie Rogêt still lives—rather than any genuine plausibility in the idea—that prompted L’Etoile to publish it and earned it a warm reception from the public. Let us examine the headings of this journal’s argument, trying to avoid the incoherence with which it was originally presented."

"The writer’s first goal is to demonstrate, by the short span between Marie’s disappearance and the discovery of the floating corpse, that the corpse could not be Marie’s. Shrinking this interval to its smallest possible length becomes, at once, the object of the reasoner’s attention. In his hasty chase after this object, he leaps to mere conjecture at the outset. ‘It is folly to suppose,’ he says, ‘that the murder—if a murder was indeed committed on her body—could have been completed quickly enough for the killers to cast the body into the river before midnight.’ We naturally ask, why? Why is it folly to suppose the murder occurred _within five minutes_ after the girl left her mother’s house? Why is it folly to suppose the murder happened at any particular time of day? Assassinations have occurred at all hours. Yet, had the murder taken place at any moment between nine o’clock on Sunday morning and a quarter to midnight, there would still have been sufficient time ‘to throw the body into the river before midnight.’ This assumption therefore amounts precisely to the claim—that the murder did not happen on Sunday at all—and, if we allow L’Etoile to make this claim, we may grant it any liberty. The paragraph beginning ‘It is folly to suppose that the murder, etc.,’ as printed in L’Etoile, can be imagined as having existed in the mind of its writer—‘It is folly to suppose that the murder, if murder was committed on the body, could have been completed soon enough to enable the murderers to cast the body into the river before midnight; it is folly, we say, to suppose all this, and at the same time, (as we are resolved to suppose,) that the body was not thrown in until after midnight’—a sentence that is sufficiently inconsequential in itself, but not as utterly absurd as the one printed.

"Were my purpose," continued Dupin, "merely to construct a case against this passage of L’Etoile’s argument, I could safely leave it where it stands."

Yet, though wretched, he is not wholly consumed by his own sorrow; rather, he throws himself earnestly into the concerns of others. He has often spoken with me about my own plans, which I have disclosed to him without concealment. He listened attentively to every argument I made for my eventual triumph and to each minute detail of the steps I had taken to secure it. Moved by the sympathy he showed, I was easily persuaded to use the language of my heart, to give voice to the fierce passion within me, and to declare, with all the fervor that warmed me, how willingly I would sacrifice my fortune, my life, my every hope, to advance my enterprise. One man's life or death seemed a trivial price for the knowledge I pursued, for the dominion I would gain and pass on over the elemental foes of our race. As I spoke, a dark gloom settled over my listener's face. At first I thought he was trying to hold back his emotion; he placed his hands before his eyes, and my voice trembled and faltered when I saw tears streaming fast between his fingers; a groan rose from his heaving chest. I paused; after a while he spoke, in broken accents: “Unhappy man! Do you share my madness? Have you also drunk the intoxicating draught? Hear me; let me tell my tale, and you will fling the cup from your lips!”

Such words, you can imagine, stirred my curiosity greatly; yet the surge of grief that seized the stranger overwhelmed his weakened strength, and many hours of rest and calm conversation were needed to restore his composure.

When he had mastered the violence of his feelings, he seemed to despise himself for being a slave to passion; having subdued the dark tyranny of despair, he turned once more to discuss me personally. He asked about the history of my early years. I recounted the story swiftly, but it awakened several lines of reflection. I spoke of my longing for a friend, of my thirst for a deeper sympathy with another mind than any I had ever known, and expressed my belief that a man could claim little happiness who lacked this blessing.

“I agree with you,” the stranger replied, “we are imperfect creatures, half‑formed; if a wiser, better, dearer friend—such a companion—were to lend his aid, he could perfect our weak and faulty natures. I once had a friend, the most noble of human beings, and therefore I feel qualified to judge friendship. You have hope, the world before you, and no cause for despair. But I—I have lost everything and cannot begin life anew.”

As he spoke, his face took on a calm, settled grief that touched me deeply. He fell silent and soon retired to his cabin.

Even broken in spirit as he is, few can feel the beauties of nature as profoundly as he does. The star‑filled sky, the sea, and every sight offered by these wondrous realms still possess the power to lift his soul from the earth. Such a man lives a double existence: he may endure misery and be crushed by disappointment, yet when he withdraws within himself, he becomes like a celestial spirit surrounded by a halo, within whose circle no sorrow or folly can enter.

Yet, although he is unhappy, he is not completely consumed by his own misery; he is deeply interested in other people's projects. He has often talked with me about mine, which I have told him plainly. He listened carefully to all my arguments about my eventual success and to every detail of the steps I had taken to achieve it. I was easily swayed by the sympathy he showed, and I used the language of my heart to express the burning passion inside me, saying with all the warmth that filled me how gladly I would sacrifice my fortune, my life, my every hope, to further my enterprise. After calming his intense feelings, he seemed to despise himself for being a slave to passion; and after quieting the dark tyranny of despair, he turned the conversation back to me personally. I was glad, too, because crabapples never taste good, and the p‑simmons wouldn’t be ripe for another two or three months.

On the fifth night after we passed St. Louis, a fierce storm broke out after midnight, with thunder, lightning, and rain falling in a solid sheet. We stayed in the wigwam and let the raft do its own thing. When the lightning flashed, we could see a long straight river ahead, flanked by high, rocky bluffs. I shouted, “Hello, Jim, look yonder!” It was a steamboat that had smashed into a rock. We were drifting straight toward it. The lightning lit her up clearly: she was leaning over, part of her upper deck still above water, every little detail visible, even a chair by the big bell with an old slouch hat hanging on its back.

But Jim was against it at first. He said, “I don’t want to go fool‑hardy on any wreck.”

The place to get canoes is where rafts lie up on the shore. But we didn’t see any rafts there, so we kept drifting for three hours or more. The night grew dark and then thick, the next worst thing to fog. You can’t make out the river’s shape, and you can’t see any distance. It grew very late and still, when a steamboat appeared up the river. We lit our lantern, hoping she’d see it. Up‑stream boats usually stay far away; they go out, follow the bars and hunt for easy water under the reefs; but on nights like this they charge straight down the channel, against the whole river.

We heard her pounding, but didn’t see her clearly until she was close. She headed right for us. Often they do that, trying to see how near they can get without touching; sometimes the wheel snaps a sweep, and the pilot sticks his head out, laughs, and thinks he’s clever. Here she came, and we thought she’d try to shave us, but she didn’t seem to be steering away. She was a big boat, coming fast, looking like a black cloud with rows of glow‑worms around it; then she bulged out, huge and frightening, with a long line of wide‑open furnace doors flashing like red‑hot teeth, and her monstrous bow and guards looming over us. While she lived, this young girl kept a scrapbook, pasting in obituaries, accidents, and accounts of patient suffering from the _Presbyterian Observer_, and she wrote poetry after them from her own mind. The verses were very good. This is what she wrote about a boy named Stephen Dowling Bots who fell down a well and drowned:

ODE TO STEPHEN DOWLING BOTS, DEC’D

And did young Stephen sicken,
And did young Stephen die?
And did the sad hearts thicken,
And did the mourners cry?

No; such was not the fate of
Young Stephen Dowling Bots;
Though sad hearts round him thickened,
’Twas not from sickness’ shots.

No whooping‑cough did rack his frame,
Nor measles drear with spots;
Not these impaired the sacred name
Of Stephen Dowling Bots.

Despised love struck not with woe
That head of curly knots,
Nor stomach troubles laid him low,
Young Stephen Dowling Bots.

O no. Then list with tearful eye,
Whilst I his fate do tell.
His soul did from this cold world fly
By falling down a well.

They got him out and emptied him;
Alas it was too late;
His spirit was gone for to sport aloft
In the realms of the good and great.

Next Sunday we all rode out to church, about three miles away, each on horseback. The men took their rifles with them, as did Buck, and kept them either between their knees or propped against the wall. The Shepherdsons did the same. The sermon was a stubborn sort—full of talk about brotherly love and the like, tiresome in its own way—but everyone said it was a good sermon. On the way home they all discussed it at length, talking about faith, good deeds, free grace, predestination, and all that sort of thing, and it struck me as one of the roughest Sundays I’d ever experienced.

About an hour after dinner, everyone was dozing—some in chairs, some in their rooms—and the place grew pretty quiet. Buck and a dog were stretched out on the grass in the sun, sound asleep. I went up to our room and decided to take a nap myself. I found sweet Miss Sophia standing in the doorway next to ours; she slipped me into her room, closed the door gently, and asked if I liked her. I said I did. She then asked me to do something for her without telling anyone, and I agreed. She said she had left her Testament in a seat at church, between two other books, and wanted me to sneak out, fetch it, and keep it secret. I said I’d do it. So I slipped out and walked up the road; there was nobody at the church except maybe a hog or two, since the door wasn’t locked, and hogs like a cool floor in summer. Most folks only go to church when they have to, but a hog is a different matter.

I thought to myself that something was odd; it wasn’t natural for a girl to be so nervous about a Testament. I gave the book a shake, and a small slip of paper fell out with “Half‑past two” penciled on it. I rifled through the book but found nothing else. I couldn’t make sense of it, so I slipped the paper back into the book. When I got home and went upstairs, Miss Sophia was waiting in her doorway. She pulled me in, shut the door, and began leafing through the Testament until she found the paper. As soon as she read it, she smiled, and before I could think, she grabbed me, gave me a squeeze, and told me I was the best boy in the world and to keep it quiet. Her face flushed red for a moment, her eyes lit up, and she looked strikingly pretty. I was quite astonished, but after catching my breath I asked what the paper meant. She asked if I had read it; I said no. She asked if I could read writing, and I replied, “No, only coarse‑hand.” She then explained that the paper was nothing more than a bookmark to hold her place, and that I could go play now.

As soon as night fell we pushed off; when we got about halfway across we left her to drift wherever the current chose. Then we lit our pipes, dangled our legs in the water, and talked about all sorts of things—we were always naked, day and night, whenever the mosquitoes would let us. The new clothes Buck’s folks had sewn for me were far too fine for comfort, and besides I never cared much for clothing.

Sometimes the whole river belonged to us for hours on end. Across the water were banks and islands, and sometimes a flicker—a candle in a cabin window—would catch the eye. Occasionally a spark or two would glint on a raft or a scow, and a fiddle or a song might drift over from one of those vessels. Living on a raft was wonderful. The sky above was peppered with stars; we would lie on our backs, stare up, and argue whether the stars were made or simply happened. Jim said they were made; I said they just happened, because it would take forever to make that many. Jim suggested the moon might have laid them, which sounded reasonable enough, so I didn’t argue—after all, I’d seen a frog lay just as many, so it must be possible. We also watched shooting stars streak across the night, and Jim thought they were spoiled and had left the nest.

Once or twice a night we’d spot a steamboat slipping by in the darkness. Every now and then she would belch a cascade of sparks from her chimneys, raining down into the river and looking beautiful. Then she’d round a bend, her lights would wink out, the noise would cease, and the river would fall silent again. After a while her wake would reach us, long after she’d vanished, nudging the raft a little, and then there would be nothing but the occasional frog croak, leaving us unable to tell how long the quiet lasted.

After midnight the people on shore went to bed, and for two or three hours the banks were black—no more cabin-window sparks. Those sparks served as our clock; the first one to appear again meant morning was near, so we would quickly find a spot to hide and tie up.

After breakfast the king produced an old, ragged deck of cards, and he and the duke played seven‑up for a spell, five cents a hand. When they grew tired they decided to "lay out a campaign," as they called it. The duke rummaged in his carpet‑bag, produced a stack of tiny printed bills, and read them aloud. One bill announced, "The celebrated Dr. Armand de Montalban, of Paris," would "lecture on the Science of Phrenology" at a certain venue on a certain day, ten cents admission, and "charts of character for twenty‑five cents each." The duke claimed that was him. Another bill named him the "world‑renowned Shakespearian tragedian, Garrick the Younger, of Drury Lane, London." Other bills listed many more names and feats—finding water and gold with a "divining‑rod," "dissipating witch spells," and the like. At length he said:

"But the histrionic muse is the darling. Have you ever trod the boards, Royalty?"

"No," replied the king.

"Then you shall, before three days pass, Fallen Grandeur," said the duke. "The first decent town we reach we'll hire a hall and stage the sword fight from Richard III and the balcony scene from Romeo and Juliet. How does that sound?"

"I'm game, up to the hub, for anything that will pay, Bilgewater; but you see, I know nothing about acting, and I've never seen much of it. I was too small when papa used to have them at the palace. Think you can teach me?"

"Easy!"

"All right. I'm just freezing for something fresh, anyway. Let's begin at once."

So the duke explained who Romeo and Juliet were, noting he was accustomed to playing Romeo, and the king could take Juliet.

"But if Juliet's such a young lass, duke, my peeled head and white whiskers might look odd beside her," the king protested.
